content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Infra engineer","url":"https://www.notion.so/2c4c370222d580299532ffc5042a1ec2","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2c4c370222d580299532ffc5042a1ec2 as of 2026-04-09T14:36:22.085Z: {"Created by":"","Created time":"2025-12-09T22:51:09.275Z","Last edited by":"","Last edited time":"2026-04-09T14:36:08.300Z","Name":"Infra engineer","url":"https://www.notion.so/2c4c370222d580299532ffc5042a1ec2"} ## Prescreen requirements Desired Profile ## Interview Plan {toggle="true"} ### 1. Conversation with TA (15 min) {toggle="true"} Topics to cover: - Ideal split b/w IC vs management - Hybrid work policy - Sanity questions to ensure eligibility - Any constraints/timing considerations - Get a feel if candidate is interviewing for right role (training infra) ### 2. Intro Call (45min) {toggle="true"} Purpose of this conversation: go through resume with candidate and try to see if candidate meets desired profile match. #### Before Interview {toggle="true"} - Review and annotate **resume** - Focus on **2 most recent positions ** - Note areas that fit into our **focus areas ** - Items to drill into - **vague** accomplishments - no tech stack, no results, massive claims or success - **“we” vs “I”** statements - did the candidate implement these? Drill and and see what portions they took on - fast hops from company to company - nothing wrong with this but might mean we should push harder on what they are looking for in their next position at the end of the interview Interview Plan #### Focus Areas {toggle="true"} - Background: - Startup/larger orgs - Frameworks: - Slurm, k8s, ray - what’s the painpoints using each framework/preference - Cluster management: - How to ensure 10k GPUs are healthy.
Active - dcgmi check - HPL test - NV bandwith tests - Storage: IOR/FIO - Networking test: NCCL, ibperf
Passive checks - Temperature - Passive GPU checks - IB flapping
- Debugging: - Has candidate shown ability to debug a difficult/vague problem on application layer and map it to infra issues: How? - Prioritization: - How does candidate select problems to work on? - Has candidate had the experience to “steer” the boat/make decisions? ### Interview Flow {toggle="true"}
Introduction (5min) "Hi \[name\], great to meet you. I'm \[your name\]. I'm on the \[team\] here at BFL, where I focus on \[responsibilities\]. I've been here \[X time\]. Today we'll spend about 45 minutes together: I'll kick things off with some technical questions, then we'll shift to a few questions about how you work with teams. I'll save the last 5 minutes for any questions you have for me. Sound good?"
"To start, could you give me a quick intro? Where you've been, what you've been working on most recently, and what drew you to this kind of role."
Resume Screen (6 min)
R1: On your resume you have \[X\]. Tell me more about your role there - what did you build, vs what was already in place/ owned by other teams?
Purpose: to gauge if this is the right pipeline:
ML Infra: training cluster ownership, NCCL, health monitoring, job scheduling
Platform/Backend: more on the developer tooling, API, distributed systems
MLOps: Primarily cluster ops - light on training specific depth
Runtime optimization: work on kernels, etc
Not a fit: background doesnt fit current pipeliine. Wrap up early if appropriate
Technical Expertise (16 min)
T1: Walk me though the most complex infrastructure project you’ve worked on. Tell me about the team, the key decisions made, and what trade-offs you navigated. (Time \~ 7min)
Follow-up probes - Why did you choose that approach over alternatives? - What did you have to sacrifice or deprioritize? - What was the hardest technical problem, and how did you debug and root-cause it?
T2: Walk me through the largest training cluster you've managed. What were the biggest challenges with job scheduling at scale, and how did you optimize resource allocation?
Listen for - Concrete cluster size (GPU count, nodes) - Specifics on scheduler (Slurm, K8s, custom) and what broke at scale - How they measured and improved utilization
T3: Tell me about a time when you had to debug why a training run worked fine with 512 GPUs but failed at 1024. What was the issue and how did you approach it?
Listen for - Structured debugging methodology - Understanding of NCCL, network topology, collective ops behavior at scale - Whether they isolate variables - can they distinguish hardware vs. software vs. config? - Is it a problem on shared resources or individual resources
Follow-up - What's your first instinct when a run fails silently vs. crashes with an error?
T4: When a multi-week training run fails, how do you balance minimizing lost progress through checkpointing vs. the performance overhead? Walk me through your decision-making process.
Listen for - Has a concrete framework - not just "checkpoint often" - Aware of checkpoint overhead (I/O, storage, step time) - Factors in MTBF, cluster reliability history, job priority
Follow-up if needed - How do you decide checkpoint frequency on a new, unknown cluster?
T5: What's your experience tuning NCCL for multi-node training? What parameters do you typically adjust and why?
Strong signal examples - NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_IB_HCA, NCCL_ALGO, NCCL_PROTO, NCCL_DEBUG - Understanding of ring vs. tree vs. NVLS algorithms - Experience profiling with NCCl tests or NCCL_DEBUG=INFO traces
Weak signal - Vague / "I mostly left defaults" without context - push for specifics
Team Fit (13 min)
F1: What are you most proud of in your career, and if you could go back, what’s one thing you’d do differently
Listen for: - Listen for self-awareness in the "what I'd change" answer - confident people acknowledge real mistakes, not just "I'd document more.”
F2: I ask every candidate this: I believe every person has a superpower - something they do distinctively better than most. What’s yours?
Notes - "I'm not looking for a job-description answer - I mean something genuinely distinctive about how you think or work." - Require a concrete example
If they give an abstract answer, say: "Can you give me a specific example of when that showed up?"
- Make sure candidate gives an example
F3: What are you wanting to grow more in your next roles? What’s something you know you need to get better at?
Notes - Distinguish genuine self-awareness from rehearsed weaknesses ("I work too hard"). A good answer names a real gap and has a plan.
F4: Describe a situation when you had to ship something that wasn't perfect because speed mattered more. How did you manage the technical debt you took on?
Listen for: - Do they acknowledge the trade-off explicitly, or did they pretend it wasn't a compromise? - Did they actually go back and address the debt, or just move on? - Did they communicate the risk to stakeholders?
- F5: Describe a situation where researchers were blocked on infrastructure. How did you prioritize the fix, and how quickly did you resolve it?
Listen for - Speed of response: did they treat researcher-blocking issues as P0? - Communication: did they keep researchers informed while investigating? - Root cause follow-through - did they prevent recurrence?
Candidate questions (5 min) "We've got about 5 minutes left - I want to make sure you have space for any questions you have for me. What's on your mind?”
### Post-interview scoring {toggle="true"}
Cluster & infrastructure depth (1 - 5) - Managed real multi-node clusters at scale - Concrete scheduler experience - Understands resource utilization bottlenecks
Debugging & root cause (1 - 5) - Structured methodology, not trial-and-error - Isolates variables systematically - Has real examples of hard bugs found
GPU perf knowledge (1 - 5) - Knows relevant benchmarks, to validate performance - Knows common failure points, and areas to focus on - Displays knowledge on working with GPU intensive workloads to a high degree
NCCL / networking knowledge (1 - 5) - Knows relevant env params and when to tune - Understands collective algorithm trade-offs - Has profiled and tuned in practice
Checkpointing & reliability (1 - 5) - Can articulate overhead vs. safety trade-off - Has a principled framework, not just intuition - Aware of failure modes at scale
Researcher partnership (1 - 5) - Treats researcher blockers as high priority - Communicates under uncertainty - Closes the loop with root cause fix
Self-awareness & growth (1- 5) - Acknowledges real trade-offs made - Names genuine gaps, not rehearsed ones - Superpower is specific and evidenced
#### Potential interviewers: {toggle="true"} 1. Saksham 2. Sandeep 3. Ian (need calibration) 4. Tatti (need calibration) 5. Scott (need calibration) 6. Luke (need calibration) ### 3. Coding Round (60min) {toggle="true"} #### Purpose of round: {toggle="true"} - Want to gauge if candidate is truly “infra obsessed” - Technically sound, and able to think with first principles - Able to prioritize tasks. - NOTE: Unless very egregious, hold more weightage on the high level solution, design philosophy, attention to detail (able to spot edge cases), and code structure, rather than the actual function implementation (pseudo code is fine) #### Ask any of these questions: {toggle="true"} 1. [Container Distribution](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1c6YRfVnOE40dylsS4HcsT_EVlhUcAmgdabVg2sa7_qk/edit?usp=drive_link) 2. [All Reduce](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZOzIt7a7to6EuLF0N1qu6ByZO8V-gVH0eG-UZIQWRSk/edit?usp=drive_link) 3. [Dupe File Finding](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1C_Xb3ZvfbYptrRRXQf3nLW6xln3m_InJTkrV0VloJz8/edit?usp=drive_link) 4. [File Streaming](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1g20Hx8HLHH3670l7LcqRLHHCw_xFVpllBUHxyi6Z1uM/edit?usp=drive_link) 5. [1F1B](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZUrlxGrJZ_xxWmk_8AkkWcSQAZjjEGyxGZMcw8a1pQ0/edit?usp=drive_link) #### Potential interviewers: {toggle="true"} 1. Sandeep 2. Ian (need calibration) 3. Tatti 4. Scott 5. Harry (need calibration) 6. Luke (need calibration) 7. Vikash (need calibration) ### 4. System Design (45 min - 1 hr) {toggle="true"}
Setting expectations (2 min) "Today is a system design interview. I'll give you a problem, and I want you to drive - treat me like a colleague you're whiteboarding with. You can ask me clarifying questions at any point; I'll answer some directly, others I'll push back to you. Here's what I care about: I want to see you think out loud. Start broad and work inward. There's no single right answer. What I'm evaluating is how you reason about trade-offs, how you handle ambiguity, and how deeply you can go when we pick a component to zoom in on. Ready?"
Select Problem track ( 40 min) #### In-house health monitoring system {toggle="true"} "Let's design an in-house health monitoring system for a GPU training cluster. We need to monitor 10,000 GPU nodes, and each node is generating metrics every 10 seconds. You have the floor - start wherever makes sense to you.”
Requirements Gathering (5-7min) > Let them drive this. Only give answers if they ask directly. If they skip this entirely and jump to design, that's a signal - note it and bring them back: "Before we get into the design, what are we actually trying to build?"

Conversely if it’s taking too long, it’s also a signal, and prompt candidate to wrap up.
Questions a strong candidate will ask - and answers you can give - "Who are the consumers of this data?" → Researchers checking job health, on-call engineers, automated alerting systems - "What's the latency requirement for detecting a failure?" → Within 30–60 seconds of a node going unhealthy - "How long do we retain metrics?" → Hot: 7 days. Cold: 90 days - "Do we need historical trend analysis or just current state?" → Both - "Are we building this from scratch or integrating with existing tools?" → Greenfield, but open to OSS - "Do we need to detect node failure, GPU failure, or both?" → Both — GPU-level granularity matters
Math they should do unprompted (bonus signal) 10,000 nodes × 1 metric/10s = 1,000 metrics/sec minimum. If 50 metrics per node: 50,000 metrics/sec — this changes the ingestion architecture significantly.
- Strong candidates estimate data volume before proposing a solution. It changes everything — a 1K/sec problem and a 50K/sec problem have different answers.
High level design (20 min)
H1: Metrics collection: what’s on the node, and how does the data get out?
What to listen for: - Push vs. pull architecture - do they justify the choice? (Push = lower latency, pull = simpler, easier backpressure) - Agent on each node (e.g. DCGM exporter, node_exporter, custom) - do they know what GPU metrics actually come from? - Do they think about what metrics matter? GPU util, memory BW, NVLink errors, ECC errors, temp, power - or do they just say "all metrics"
**Probe if shallow** - "What metrics specifically are you collecting, and how do you decide what's important vs. noise?" - "How do you handle a node that stops sending metrics - is that itself a signal?"
Positives - Knows GPU-specific metrics (DCGM, NVLink, ECC) - Missing heartbeat = failure signal
Negatives - Just says "Prometheus" without justifying
H2: Ingestion and storage: How do you handle 50K+ metrics/sec reliably?
What to listen for - Do they introduce a buffer/queue layer between collection and storage, or go direct? - Storage engine choice - TSDB (Prometheus, InfluxDB, VictoriaMetrics, Thanos) - can they explain why TSDB vs. general-purpose DB? - Hot/cold tiering - do they think about cost/retention unprompted?
Probe if shallow - "What happens if your ingestion pipeline falls behind - how do you prevent metric loss?" - "Why not just use PostgreSQL or S3 directly?"
Positives - Buffer layer for backpressure - Justifies TSDB choice with compression/query patterns
H3: Health checks - passive (metrics) vs active (probes). How do you balance them?
What to listen for - Passive: metric thresholds, anomaly detection on telemetry stream - non-disruptive - Active: synthetic workloads, NCCL tests, compute/memory benchmarks - disruptive, can impact running jobs - Do they think about when to run active checks? (Pre-job, post-job, scheduled maintenance windows - not mid-training)
- Continuous vs. triggered - is there a state machine for node health?
Probe - "If a GPU is running fine on passive metrics but a job fails - how does that trigger a deeper active check?"
Positives - Explicit active/passive split with scheduling awareness - Node health as a state machine (healthy → suspect → quarantined)
Negatives - Active checks run mid-job - they'd cause failures
H4: Alerting and dashboards - how does a human know something is wrong?
What to listen for - Alerting: threshold-based vs. anomaly-based vs. both - do they understand the false-positive/false-negative trade-off? - Alert routing - who gets paged? Researcher vs. on-call infra eng vs. automated remediation? - Dashboard layers: cluster-wide health (fleet view) vs. per-job health vs. per-node drilldown
Probe - "If 50 nodes go unhealthy simultaneously, how do you avoid alert storms?" - "How do researchers know their specific job's nodes are healthy without paging on-call?"
Deep Dive - pick 1 component (20 min) "Let's go deep on one area. Where do you want to focus - ingestion pipeline, the health state machine, or the active check system?" Let them choose - their choice signals where they're most confident.
D1: Ingestion pipeline - "Walk me through exactly what happens from the moment a GPU emits a metric to when it appears in a dashboard." - "Where can this pipeline drop data - and how do you detect and recover from each failure point?" - "How do you scale from 10K to 100K nodes without redesigning the pipeline?" - "What does a rolling deploy of the collection agent look like across 10K nodes?"
D2: Health state machine - "Walk me through all the states a node can be in and what triggers transitions." - "If a node flaps between healthy and suspect, how do you avoid thrashing the scheduler?" - "How do you distinguish a truly unhealthy GPU from a noisy metric?" - "If a job fails on a node, who decides the node is at fault vs. the job code?"
D3: Active check system - "What does an active check actually run - what's the test?" - "How do you run NCCL tests across 1000 nodes without impacting running jobs?" - "What's the SLA for validating a newly provisioned node before jobs can land on it?" - "How do you store and trend active check results over time to catch degrading hardware?"
#### Design a scheduling system for research jobs {toggle="true"} "Let's design a job scheduling system for ML research. It needs to support 100 parallel jobs, each taking anywhere from 30 minutes to 8 hours. Jobs are queueable, have priorities, access datasets in the hundreds of TB, and researchers need to monitor and cancel them. You have the floor.”
Requirements Gathering (5-7min) > Let them drive this. Only give answers if they ask directly. If they skip this entirely and jump to design, that's a signal - note it and bring them back: "Before we get into the design, what are we actually trying to build?"

Conversely if it’s taking too long, it’s also a signal, and prompt candidate to wrap up.
Questions a strong candidate will ask - and answers you can give - "Who submits jobs - researchers via API, CLI, or UI?" → All three, prioritize API-first - "What's the compute substrate - bare metal GPUs, k8s, Slurm, cloud?" → Bare metal GPU cluster, custom scheduler
"How many GPUs per job — fixed or variable?" → Variable, 1 to 512 GPUs per job - "What does priority mean - is it user-set, team-set, or automatic?" → Users set per-job, teams have base quota - "What happens to a preempted job - lost progress or resume from checkpoint?" → Should support checkpoint-and-resume where possible - BONUS: If candidate can identify that there are some workloads that are embarrassingly parallel/ don’t need much statefulness, and hence can run as background/whenever idle compute is available - "How big are the images (up to 5GB) - do we pre-pull or pull at runtime?" → Pre-pull to avoid cold-start latency
Math they should do unprompted (bonus signal) 100TB dataset ÷ 100Gbps network = \~8 seconds to stream 1GB. If job accesses 10TB, that's 800s just for data I/O — which means data locality and caching matter architecturally.
High level design (20 min)
H1: Job lifecycle - submission, state machine, completion
What to listen for - Do they enumerate the full state machine? (submitted → queued → scheduled → running → completed/failed/cancelled) - Do they think about idempotency in submission — what if the user submits twice? - How does cancellation propagate — graceful shutdown vs. SIGKILL? Does it free resources atomically?
Probe - "If a job transitions from running to failed — what cleans up its resources and when?" - "How do you ensure a job that fails mid-way doesn't leave orphaned GPU allocations?"
Positives - Full state machine with transitions - Cleanup is an explicit step, not assumed
Negatives: - Only happy path — fails to mention failure states
H2: Scheduler & priority queue - how do you decide what runs next?
What to listen for - Priority + fairness - do they see that pure priority leads to starvation? Do they introduce aging or quota? - Gang scheduling - for multi-GPU jobs, all nodes must be available simultaneously - this is hard. Do they surface it? - Preemption - can a high-priority job bump a running lower-priority job? At what cost?
Probe - "A P0 job needs 512 GPUs but the cluster is full. What options do you have?" - "Two teams both have P1 jobs - how do you prevent one team from starving the other?"
Positives - Surfaces gang scheduling problem unprompted - Priority + fairness, not just priority - Preemption with checkpoint awareness
Negatives - Pure FIFO or pure priority with no starvation protection
H3: Data access - 100s of TB of datasets. How do jobs get their data?
What to listen for - Dataset locality - do they think about caching datasets on nodes vs. streaming from central storage every time? - Image pre-pull strategy. Pulling at job start = massive latency. When and where do they pre- pull? - Storage layer choice - NFS, Lustre, object store (S3-compatible), RDMA - and trade-offs for each at this scale
Probe - "If 50 jobs start simultaneously and all try to pull the same 5GB image - what happens?" - "How does the scheduler use data locality as a placement signal?"
Positives - Dataset caching / locality-aware scheduling - Image registry with pre-pull daemonset or equivalent
Negatives - Mentions NFS without noting its scalability ceiling
H4: Failure handling - job fails, node fails, network partition.
What to listen for - Retry semantics - automatic retry? How many times? Does the user set this? - Checkpoint-and-resume - does the system know where to resume, or does the job own that? - Node failure during job - how does the scheduler detect it and what's the recovery path?
Probe - "A job has been running for 6 hours and one of its 128 nodes goes down. What happens?" - "How do you distinguish a job that failed due to bad hardware vs. bad code?"
Positives - Clear retry contract with user-configurable limits - Checkpoint integration in failure path - Hardware fault attribution separate from job failure
Deep Dive - pick 1 component (20 min) > "Let's zoom in. Where do you want to go deep - the scheduler algorithm, the job state store, or the data access layer?" Let them choose.
D1: Scheduler algorithm - "Walk me through exactly how your scheduler selects which nodes a job lands on." - "How does your scheduler handle a job that needs 512 GPUs when only 400 are free?" - "What's the time complexity of your scheduling algorithm as queue depth grows?" - How do you prevent the scheduler from becoming a bottleneck at 1000 queued jobs?"
D2: Job state score - "Walk me through the data model for a job - what fields, what indexes, what guarantees?" - "How do you ensure a job is never lost - not in the queue, not mid-transition?" - "If the scheduler process crashes mid-assignment - what happens to jobs in flight?" - "How do you serve the status API at low latency without hammering your job store?"
D3: Data access layer - "How does a node know which datasets it needs before the job starts?" - "If a dataset is 50TB and your node has 20TB of local cache - what's your eviction policy?" - "How do you handle a dataset that's being written to while jobs are reading from it?" - "If cache misses cause a job to run 3x slower - how would you detect and surface that?"
Candidate questions (3 min) "That was a really solid discussion. I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?"
### **Post-interview scoring** {toggle="true"}
Requirements gathering (1 - 5) - Did they clarify before designing? Did they do scale math unprompted? - Asked who, what, scale before drawing boxes - Estimated data volume / throughput - Surfaced ambiguity rather than assuming
High-level design quality (1 - 5) - Was the component decomposition sensible? Were trade-offs named, not just choices? - Correct components for the problem - Trade-offs articulated, not just conclusions - Design matches the stated requirements
Deep dive depth (1 - 5) - When pushed on one component, could they go multiple levels deep with correctness? - Held up under specific technical questions - Knew the limits of their own design - Answered at implementation level, not just concept
Failure & edge case thinking (1 - 5) - Did they design for failure, or just the happy path? - Named failure modes unprompted - Recovery paths are explicit, not assumed - Partial failure handled (not just total failure)
Candidate drove the interview (1 - 5) - Did they lead, or wait to be asked for each next thing? - Moved between phases without prompting - Made decisions and justified them - Asked smart clarifying questions
Production thinking (bonus) (1 - 5) - Did they volunteer observability, cost, or CI/CD without being asked? - Named specific metrics / SLOs - Thought about cost / GPU utilization - Addressed safe deployment unprompted
#### Potential interviewers: {toggle="true"} 1. Sandeep 2. Saksham 3. Ian (need calibration) 4. Tatti (need calibration) 5. Harry (need calibration) ### 5. Onsite (5 - 6 hr) {toggle="true"} Stages: #### Technical Deep Dive & Retro (45 min - 1 hr) {toggle="true"}
Setting the stage (5 min) Here's how we'll structure it: you'll have about 15 minutes to walk me through the project uninterrupted - the architecture, the key decisions you made, the trade-offs, and the challenges. I won't cut in during that time. After that, I'll go deep with questions for about 20 minutes. Then we'll end with a retro - how you'd approach it differently today. We'll save the last 5 minutes for your questions. Any questions before we start?"

"Go ahead - take a moment to think about which project you want to walk me through. It should be something where you made meaningful technical decisions and faced real constraints. Ready when you are." "Hi \[name\], welcome. I'm \[your name\] - I'm on \[team\], focused on \[responsibilities\]. Today's format is a bit different from a typical interview. I want to hear you go really deep on one project - the most technically complex thing you've worked on, ideally in the ML infrastructure space. No slides needed; I care about the substance, not the presentation.
Candidate Presentation (15 min) > Do not interrupt during this phase. Your job is to listen and take notes. If they go off on a tangent, let them - it often reveals what they actually care about. If they finish early (under 8 min), that's a signal in itself.
What to listen for? - Depth markers - note when you hear these - Do they lead with "what" or "why"? Strong candidates explain reasoning before mechanics. - Do they name specific systems, numbers, constraints - or stay at abstract level? - Do they acknowledge trade-offs unprompted, or present everything as the obvious right call? - Do they mention other teams, stakeholders, pushback? Or present as if they worked in a vacuum? - How do they talk about failure? Do they surface it voluntarily, minimize it, or skip it entirely? - Note-taking prompts (jot for Q&A) - Any decision they made that sounds under-explained - you'll push on this - Any number that sounds impressive - verify it. - Any team dynamic they glossed over - ask about it - Any technology choice that wasn't justified — surface it
Deep Q&A ( \~ 20 min) ”Thanks - really interesting. I'm going to go deep now. Some of my questions will be about things you mentioned, some will push into areas you didn't cover. There are no trick questions - I just want to understand how you think.”
Q1: Architecture and design decisions - “You chose \[X\]. Walk me through why that over \[Y\]”
Frame it as - "You mentioned \[decision\]. What were the real alternatives you considered, and what ruled them out?" - "At the time, what were you most uncertain about in that choice?" - "If someone on your team pushed back on that approach, what would their strongest argument have been?"
Listen for - Can they steelman the alternative? Weak candidates can only defend their choice, not articulate the opponent's case. - Is their reasoning based on data/constraints, or post-hoc rationalization? - Positives: - Names concrete constraints that drove the choice - Acknowledges what they gave up - Negatives: - Every choice was "obvious" or "best practice"
Q2: Scale and constraints - “What broke first as this scaled, and how did you know it was going to break before it did?”
Variations - "What were the hard limits of your design - the ceiling you knew you'd eventually hit?" - "What assumptions in your architecture would have needed to change at 10x the load?" - "How did you validate it would hold at scale before you committed to it?"
Listen for - Do they have mental models for failure modes, or did they discover problems reactively? - Can they distinguish what they knew vs. what they discovered?
Positives - Anticipates bottlenecks before they happened - Has numbers - not just "it scaled well"
- Negatives - Can only describe what broke, not why it was going to
Q3: Hardest technical problem - “What was the single hardest problem you hit, and walk me through how you actually solved it step by step”
Push on process, not just outcome - "Walk me through your debugging process - what did you try first, what eliminated what?" - "What was your hypothesis going in, and when did it turn out to be wrong?" - "How long did it take, and what eventually cracked it?"
Listen for - Do they have a systematic method, or did they stumble into the answer? - Can they reconstruct their mental state at the time - not just the clean retrospective version?
Positives: - Describes what they ruled out and why - Admits they were wrong initially
Negatives - Solution arrived via luck or someone else - worth noting - Jumps straight to answer with no process
Q4: Team & cross-functional dynamics - “How many teams were involved, and where did you hit the most friction?”
Variations - "Who pushed back hardest on your approach, and what was their concern?" - "How did you get alignment when teams had different priorities or timelines?" - "Was there a decision you made that someone else owned - how did you navigate that?"
Listen for - Do they talk about people and dynamics specifically, or abstractly? ("we aligned" vs. how they actually aligned) - Do they acknowledge that others had valid concerns, or were all dissenters just wrong?
Positives - Names the person/team and their actual concern - Describes influence without authority
Negatives - Everyone agreed, no pushback - suspicious - Dismissive of other teams' concerns
Q5: Ownership depth - “Which parts of this did you personally design vs inherit or implement someone else’s spec?”
Push if needed - "On \[specific component\] - were you the one who decided on that approach, or were you executing on a direction that was already set?" - "If this project had gone sideways, which parts would have been on you?"
Listen for - Honest ownership vs. claiming credit for the team's work. This usually reveals itself in specificity - real owners have opinions on the details.
Positives - Can say "I didn't decide X, that was \[person\]" - Has strong opinions on their own scope
Negatives - Fuzzy on what they personally contributed
Retro: What they’d do differently with today’s knowledge (12 min) "Let's shift into retro mode. Forget what was possible at the time - if you were starting this project today, with everything you now know, how would you do it differently? I'm interested in both the technical choices and how you'd run the project.”
R1: Technical retro: “What’s the one architectural decision you’d reverse, and what would you replace it with?”
Push past surface-level answers - "Is that something you would have known at the time if you'd had more information, or did it require the experience of running it?" - "What did you learn from that mistake that you've applied since?"
Watch out for - "I'd document better" or "I'd write more tests" - these are safe answers that signal low self-awareness. Push: "Okay, but technically - what would you actually change about the design?" - Strong answers name a specific design choice, explain why it was wrong, and describe concretely what they'd replace it with - including the new trade-offs that introduces.
R2: Process retro: “How would you run the project differently - team structure, decision making, how you handled uncertainty?”
Variations - "Were there decisions that took too long to make? What slowed them down?" - "Looking back, what did you learn too late - what signal did you have early but didn't act on?" - "Was there a moment where the team's morale or alignment broke down? What would you do differently there?"
Listen for - Genuine retrospection vs. corporate retrospection ("we could have communicated better"). - Strong candidates name specific moments and specific people.
R3: Growth signal: “What did this project teach you that you couldn’t have learned any other way?”
Listen for: - Intellectual honesty - do they credit the project for real learning, or just recount accomplishments?\\ - Transfer - have they actually applied what they learned, or just identified it?
Positives: - Names a belief they held that turned out to be wrong - Points to how it changed their next project
Negatives: - Lessons are generic ("importance of communication")
Candidate questions (5 min) "That was a really good discussion - I have what I need. We've got about 5 minutes. What questions do you have for me?”
### **Post-interview scoring** {toggle="true"}
Technical depth & correctness (1 - 5) - Did the project actually warrant t he complexity they described? - Were the technical claims accurate under pressure? - Specificity held up when probed - Correct mental models for the domain - Numbers checked out
Design decision quality (1 - 5) - Were their choices well-reasoned, or lucky/inherited? Could they articulate trade-offs and steelman alternatives? - Choices grounded in real constraints - Can argue the opposing view - Acknowledges what they gave up
Debugging & problem-solving (1 - 5) - Did they have a systematic process? Can they reconstruct how they thought through a hard problem, not just the answer? - Structured elimination, not trial-and-error - Admits wrong hypotheses - Process is repeatable, not luck
Ownership clarity (1 - 5) - Was this genuinely their work? Do they know the difference between "I built this" and "I was on the team that built this"? - Honest about scope of own contribution - Strong opinions on details they owned - Can say "that wasn't me" cleanly
Cross-team & stakeholder navigation (1 - 5) - Do they understand that hard projects are also people problems? - Can they describe influence without authority? - Names specific friction and how they resolved it - Acknowledges valid concerns from others - Doesn't dismiss disagreement
Self-awareness & learning (1 - 5) - Did the retro reveal someone who actually reflects and improves, or someone who performs reflection? - Names a belief they held that was wrong - Retro is specific, not generic - Can connect learning to later work

## **Member of Technical Staff - Core Infrastructure / API Backend Engineer**
Freiburg (Germany), San Francisco (USA)
**What if the gap between a breakthrough research model and something millions of people can actually use is making inference fast enough and APIs reliable enough to matter?**
Our founding team pioneered Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion - breakthroughs that made generative AI accessible to millions. Today, our FLUX models power creative tools, design workflows, and products across industries worldwide.
Our FLUX models are best-in-class not only for their capability, but for ease of use in developing production applications. We top public benchmarks and compete at the frontier - and in most instances we're winning.
If you're relentlessly curious and driven by high agency, we want to talk.
With a team of \~80, we move fast and punch above our weight. From our labs in Freiburg - a university town in the Black Forest - and San Francisco, we're building what comes next.
But here's what doesn't show up in download numbers: transforming research models into production systems that serve millions of requests reliably. Models that generate in seconds, not minutes. APIs that don't fall over under load. Demos that convince people this technology is real. That's the infrastructure you'll build.
**What You'll Pioneer**
You'll be the bridge between research breakthroughs and production reality. This isn't about maintaining existing APIs—it's about taking models fresh from research, deploying them on robust serving infrastructure, and making them as reliable as possible so we can always show the world what's possible.
**You'll be the person who:**
Develops and maintains world class robust cloud architecture to serve machine learning models at scale.
You maintain the highest standard for operational excellence ensuring high availability and reliability of model serving infrastructure—downtime means users can't create
**Questions We're Wrestling With**
How do you make diffusion model inference fast enough for interactive experiences without sacrificing quality?
What's the right serving architecture for models that don't fit standard deployment patterns?
How do you balance multiple models while ensuing efficient use of compute resources
How do you build code that is both reliable in production but also enables fast iteration on new product ideas and customer POCs
What does "production-ready" actually mean for models that are still actively being improved?
How do you instrument systems to understand not just that they're working, but how well they're working for users?
These aren't theoretical—they're tradeoffs you'll navigate daily as research becomes product.
**Who Thrives Here**
Self driven and performance obsessed engineers. You are never satisfied with the status quo and will push operational excellence to the next level
**You likely have:**
Strong proficiency in Python
Extensive experience with RESTful API development —you've built APIs that real products depend on
Familiarity with containerization and orchestration technologies (Docker, Kubernetes) for deploying infrastructure at scale
Knowledge of cloud platforms (AWS, GCP, or Azure) and IAC
Experience with distributed task queues and scalable model serving architectures 
Understanding of monitoring, logging, and observability best practices for multi region cloud architecture 
Implemented CI/CD systems that quickly test and deploy code globally
**We'd be especially excited if you:**
Familiarity with MLOps practices and tools
Know database systems and data streaming technologies
Have experience with A/B testing and feature flagging in production environments
Understand security best practices for API development and ML model serving
Have built real-time inference systems with low-latency optimizations
**What We're Building Toward**
We're not just serving models—we're building the infrastructure that makes frontier AI research usable at scale. Every optimization you ship makes inference faster. Every API you build enables new applications. If that sounds more compelling than maintaining existing systems, we should talk.

content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"🔐 Infra/Security & compliance","url":"https://www.notion.so/1c7c370222d580dd9167d7307f100abd","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/1c7c370222d580dd9167d7307f100abd as of 2025-04-03T09:22:12.694Z: {"title":"Infra/Security & compliance"} ### **1. Where are we spending disproportionate time troubleshooting?** We’re in firefighting mode too often—handling \~1 production incident per day, mostly infra-related (e.g., outages, latency). ### **2. Which critical projects have insufficient attention?** - **Infra Stability:** We need root-cause analysis and hardening to cut incident frequency—think better monitoring, chaos testing, or capacity planning. It’s foundational but neglected. - **Cloud Security Posture:** Wiz and Vanta will be live, but we need to implement controls and leverage it fully—automated remediation and policy enforcement cannot be on the back burner. - **API Security:** Daily incidents leave no bandwidth for deeper API testing. We have engaged third party for this already, and will have to coordinate. - **Compliance Automation:** SOC 2/ISO 27001—proactive automation. ### **3. What tasks are being done by people too senior for them?** Just a couple of things. I’m stuck in the weeds more than I should be: - **Vendor questionnaire Reviews:** Chasing HyperComply follow-ups—operational, not strategic. But I have a plan to make it self-sufficient and get myself out of this by the end of April. - **Basic Hardening:** I’d rather spend designing resilient architecture. ### **4. What skills do we lack for upcoming priorities?** Given our incident rate and roadmap, we’re missing: - **Infra Reliability + Security:** Someone who can debug production issues (e.g., Kubernetes, AWS) and secure the stack (e.g., Terraform, Wiz integrations). - **Automation Chops:** Scripting skills to offload repetitive tasks—incident playbooks, compliance automation, alert triage. - **API Security:** Expertise in securing APIs under load—threat modeling, runtime monitoring. - **Compliance Workflow:** Practical knowledge of SOC 2/ISO 27001 to streamline audits without my constant oversight. ### **Hiring Needs (Next 6 Months)** I’d push for one hybrid role—a **Security & Reliability Engineer**: - **Must-Haves:** Infra/backend experience (e.g., Azure, Kubernetes), scripting (e.g., Python, Bash), and comfort with security/compliance basics. - **Nice-to-Haves:** API security, familiarity with Wiz/Vanta/HyperComply, incident response experience. - **Why One Role:** We need a versatile player who can fight fires, harden infra, support compliance, and also roll sleeves and make code changes—reducing our tactical load so we can focus on architecture, API security, and scaling strategy. A second resource might stretch us thin at this stage, but we can revisit it in 6 months. ### **Automation & Outsourcing Opportunities** - **Automate:** - [ ] Incident response playbooks (e.g., auto-restart scripts, Wiz remediation triggers). - [ ] Compliance evidence pipelines (e.g., Vanta API to pull logs). - [ ] Monitoring/alert consolidation—less noise, faster triage. - **Outsource:** - [x] Vendor reviews via HyperComply or a managed service—low-hanging fruit. - [x] External pentests—annual or semi-annual, to cover APIs/infra without taxing us. - **In-House Priority:** Infra stability, security, and API protection must stay internal—too core to our product and too tied to daily ops. **Profile** - Beyond the technical skills (infra, security, automation), we need someone comfortable with the non-glamorous “grunt work”—think manual incident triage, chasing compliance evidence, or willing to interact with auditors/vendors—especially in our current high-incident environment. - Not every candidate enjoys that, but it’s critical until we automate more (e.g., evidence pipelines alert workflows). I suggest we bring this upfront during interviews? I’d rather set clear expectations than backfill later. Let me know what you think! Next step: - Arun to help with JD ![]() "}

title: Infrastructure Engineer — Hiring Guide
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Infrastructure Engineer — Hiring Guide ","url":"https://www.notion.so/30ac370222d580a58e20e697f506c23d","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/30ac370222d580a58e20e697f506c23d as of 2026-04-08T05:59:28.905Z: {"title":"**Infrastructure Engineer — Hiring Guide
**"} Infrastructure Engineer — JD **Team:** Infrastructure / Research Platform **Goal of this hire:** Build and operate the infrastructure that powers training and research, including cluster health, performance, observability, and reliability across large GPU fleets. **Why now:** As research demands grow, we need more infrastructure depth to keep systems reliable, performant, and scalable without slowing down model development. **Open Headcount:** We need people to join our research efforts — one based in the EU and one in the US. Both roles are focused on setting up and monitoring the cluster to ensure our large production runs and data processing pipelines run smoothly. A key part of the mandate is building and maintaining robust observability layers around our infrastructure so we can proactively detect issues, track performance, and keep research unblocked. --- ## Ideal Candidate Profile (ICP) ### Must-Haves (Non-Negotiables) - Strong hands-on experience working with GPUs (training or infra side) - Experience debugging performance issues in GPU systems (utilization, bottlenecks, failures) - Ability to read logs and trace issues across systems (GPU, infra, application) - Strong understanding of distributed systems or large-scale infrastructure - High ownership — able to identify problems and drive solutions independently ### Strong Signals (What “great” looks like) - Experience with GPU performance tuning (benchmarking, utilization, throughput) - Familiarity with NCCL or similar GPU communication/debugging tools - Experience identifying bottlenecks in training systems (GPU starvation, I/O, networking) - Proven ability to proactively find issues (not just respond to incidents) - Works effectively under pressure and can debug issues in real-time - Experience working closely with research / ML teams - Strong curiosity and drive to learn new systems quickly ### Archetype 1: GPU / Training Performance Engineer - Deep understanding of GPU systems and performance (GPU burn, utilization, benchmarking) - Experience debugging NCCL / multi-GPU training issues - Focus on improving training performance and efficiency - Able to quickly identify and fix bottlenecks impacting training speed - Some experience with challenges involved data movement, be it for training, processing, or checkpointing 1. Understands how to leverage the memory hierarchy effectively (object, lustre, NFS, NVME, on chip memory) ### Archetype 2: Infrastructure / Cluster & Observability Engineer - Experience managing large-scale clusters (Kubernetes, Slurm, or similar) - Strong monitoring and observability experience (Prometheus, Grafana, dashboards) - Experience building internal tooling for reliability and debugging - Handles node health, failures, and cluster-level issues (triage, automation) - Focus on making infrastructure stable, observable, and scalable ### Nice-to-Haves - Experience with Kubernetes or Slurm - Experience managing large GPU clusters - Experience with infrastructure cost/performance tradeoffs - Experience building internal tooling for engineering teams - Experience with multi-cloud or hybrid environments ### Not a Fit - Pure backend/API engineers without infrastructure or GPU experience - Data pipeline / analytics-focused profiles - ML researchers without hands-on infrastructure or performance ownership - DevOps engineers without experience debugging systems at scale --- ## Candidate Archetypes Typical Profiles That Fit - GPU / Training Performance Engineer (GPU utilization, benchmarking, NCCL, training bottlenecks) - Cluster / Infrastructure Engineer (Kubernetes, Slurm, cluster management, reliability) - Observability / Platform Engineer (Prometheus, Grafana, dashboards, monitoring systems) - Startup Infrastructure Generalist (0→1 builder, owns infra end-to-end, strong debugging mindset) --- ## **Interview Process** #### **Initial Screen + Technical Discussion (45 min)** {toggle="true"} Initial call + technical discussion — Interview Guide (Infrastructure) Goal: - Evaluate hands-on experience with infrastructure, GPUs, and debugging systems at scale - Confirm baseline fit and interest - Validate high-level experience with infrastructure and GPUs #### **Coding (60 min)** {toggle="true"} Coding — Interview Guide (Infrastructure) Goal: - Validate baseline engineering ability and problem solving It will be a 60-minute coding interview focused on distributed systems thinking applied to ML infrastructure. The assessment can be attempted in any coding language, and is not a typical leetcode-esque question, rather more practical on problems faced representative of the role. #### **System Design (45 min) \[NOTE if strong yes in past rounds, will run this during onsite\]** {toggle="true"} System Design (Infrastructure) Goal: - Evaluate high-level system design thinking across reliability, scalability, and architecture #### Onsite {toggle="true"} Technical Project Discussion (60 min) Technical Project Discussion — Interview Guide (Infrastructure) Goal: - Evaluate ownership, decision-making, and depth of past technical work Onsite Coding Assessment (2-3 hrs) Onsite Coding Assessment (Infrastructure) Behavioral / Research Discussion (30 min) Behavioral / Research — Interview Guide (Infrastructure) Goal: - Evaluate collaboration with researchers and ability to work across teams Culture Fit (30 min)
**Culture Fit — Interview Guide (Infrastructure)** Goal: - Evaluate ownership, motivation, and alignment with BFL working style --- ## **Interview Ownership & Coverage** Technical Discussion(45 min)

## Detailed Descriptions & Sample Prompts --- ## PRE-training Source: `configs/projects/2025_11_flux2_klein/data.yaml` ### pumpkin (512, 768) **Path:** `object://image-datasets/single/pumpkin/` tars: `res_512/`, `res_768/` \| **Weight:** 0.15 each \| **Captions:** `meta_captions_long_joy` (JoyCaption VLM) \| **Filters:** watermark\<0.3, NSFW\<0.4, excludes eyeem/alamy/getty/istockonline Pumpkin is the foundational pre-training corpus for the Flux/Klein diffusion model. In the pre-training phase, it serves lower-resolution buckets (512px and 768px), providing broad visual coverage to teach the model basic image structure, composition, and text-image alignment. Each sample consists of a single image with a caption generated by the JoyCaption VLM, which produces detailed, long-form descriptive captions by combining the original web-scraped caption with visual understanding. The captioning prompt instructs the VLM to describe the image in a sentence, mentioning actions, style (if not a photo), specific product names, artists, or photographers from the original caption. Pre-training filters exclude images from specific stock-photo domains and enforce quality thresholds. A validation split is excluded via `validation_res_all.txt`. This is pure T2I training with no reference images. Captions always begin with “This image shows.” **Sample Prompts:**
1. “This image shows a golden retriever sitting on a grassy hillside at sunset, its fur illuminated by the warm golden-hour light, with rolling green hills and scattered wildflowers in the background.”
2. “This image shows a minimalist flat-lay photograph of a ceramic coffee cup, a leather-bound journal, and a fountain pen arranged on a marble countertop, shot from directly above in a clean editorial style.”
3. “This image shows a vibrant street art mural depicting a stylized phoenix in neon colors painted on a weathered brick wall in an urban alley, with a fire escape and parked bicycle visible to the right.”
4. “This image shows a close-up portrait photograph of an elderly man with deep wrinkles and kind blue eyes wearing a wool flat cap, photographed in natural window light with a shallow depth of field.”
5. “This image shows a digital illustration of a fantasy castle perched on a floating island above clouds, with waterfalls cascading from its edges and a dragon circling one of its spires, in a detailed concept art style.” --- ## MID-training Source: `configs/projects/2025_11_flux2_klein/data.yaml` ### pumpkin (1024hr) **Path:** `object://image-datasets/single/pumpkin/` tar: `res_1024hr/` \| **Weight:** 0.30 \| **Captions:** `gpt5_captions` (detailed/long/short), `meta_captions_pixtral` The mid-training variant of pumpkin uses the highest-resolution bucket (1024px+) of the same curated web-scraped dataset, transitioning the model to higher-fidelity generation. Captions come from two parquet aspects: `gpt5_captions` (producing three variants – detailed, long, and short) and `meta_captions_pixtral` (quality scores). During loading, `midtraining_prepare` randomly selects among the three caption variants with equal probability, unless the detailed caption contains quotation marks (indicating specific text content), in which case it is always used. The same domain-level filters and quality thresholds apply. This is the highest-weighted single dataset in the mixture at 0.30, and also serves as the T2I validation split (held-out via `validation_res_1024hr.txt`). The shift to higher resolution and multi-granularity captions trains the model to produce detailed, coherent outputs at production quality. **Sample Prompts:**
1. *(detailed)* “A professional food photograph of an artfully plated seared salmon fillet on a bed of wilted spinach and quinoa, garnished with microgreens and a drizzle of balsamic reduction, presented on a white ceramic plate atop a rustic wooden table.”
2. *(long)* “A panoramic landscape photograph of the Dolomites mountain range in northern Italy during autumn, with golden larch trees in the foreground and dramatic jagged peaks rising into a cloud-streaked sky at golden hour.”
3. *(short)* “A black cat sitting on a windowsill at night.”
4. *(detailed)* “A highly detailed digital painting of a cyberpunk cityscape at night, featuring towering neon-lit skyscrapers, holographic billboards advertising in Japanese characters, rain-slicked streets reflecting the colored lights, and a solitary figure in a hooded jacket walking beneath a transparent umbrella.”
5. *(long)* “An aerial drone photograph of a winding coastal road along dramatic sea cliffs, with turquoise waves crashing against dark volcanic rock and a red convertible car visible on the curve.” --- ### complex_poses **Path:** `object://image-datasets/single/complex-poses/` \| **Weight:** 0.06 \| **Captions:** `meta_df_2025-10-08T15-08-55` (detailed/long/short) \| **Filters:** NSFW\<0.4 A curated dataset specifically designed to improve the model’s ability to generate human figures in challenging, non-standard body poses – a known weakness in diffusion models. Captions follow the same three-granularity format as pumpkin_mid, selected with equal probability via `midtraining_prepare`. The dataset applies a simpler NSFW filter without watermark or domain-exclusion filters, suggesting the source data is pre-filtered. A config comment notes it is “currently still medium resolution.” At 0.06 weight, it serves as targeted data augmentation for dynamic, unusual, or physically challenging poses (e.g., acrobatics, dance, martial arts, yoga, sports action shots). **Sample Prompts:**
1. *(detailed)* “A professional sports photograph of a female gymnast mid-rotation during a floor exercise, her body fully extended in a layout position with arms swept back and toes pointed.”
2. *(long)* “A break-dancer performing a windmill on a cardboard-covered street corner, spinning on his shoulders with legs extended in a wide V-shape, surrounded by onlookers.”
3. *(short)* “A yoga practitioner in crow pose on a beach.”
4. *(detailed)* “A dramatic action photograph of a parkour athlete leaping between two concrete buildings, captured in mid-air with his body horizontally stretched, one arm reaching for the far ledge.”
5. *(long)* “A contemporary dancer arching backward into a deep backbend on a wooden stage, her long hair sweeping the floor while one arm reaches skyward under a single spotlight.” --- ### squash **Path:** `object://image-datasets/single/squash/` \| **Weight:** 0.06 \| **Captions:** `api_captions` (detailed always used) A curated, pre-filtered single-image dataset with `api_captions` (API-based model captions producing three granularity levels). A notable distinction: for squash, the detailed caption is **always** used (bypassing random selection), suggesting the dataset benefits from highly specific descriptions. The comment “should be prefiltered already” means no additional watermark or NSFW filtering is applied at load time. The prelist file (`source_ids_api_captions.txt`) gates the dataset to captioned samples only. This dataset likely contains high-quality, diverse photographic or artistic images curated for specific visual qualities not well-represented in pumpkin. **Sample Prompts:**
1. “A meticulously arranged still life photograph featuring a clear glass vase of white peonies, a stack of vintage hardcover books, and a brass pocket watch on an antique mahogany desk. The soft, diffused natural light enters from a window on the left.”
2. “A wide-angle architectural photograph of the interior of a modern art museum, showcasing clean white walls, polished concrete floors, and a large abstract sculpture in brushed steel at the center of the atrium.”
3. “A close-up macro photograph of a honeybee covered in yellow pollen grains, perched on the stamen of a bright purple lavender flower. The shallow depth of field renders the garden background into a soft bokeh.”
4. “A cinematic still of a narrow cobblestone alley in an old European city at twilight, with warm amber light spilling from wrought-iron street lamps, ivy climbing stone walls, and a solitary red bicycle leaning against a wooden door.”
5. “A high-resolution product photograph of a pair of handcrafted leather boots on a rough slate surface, shot at a slight angle with studio lighting that emphasizes the grain texture, double stitching, and brass eyelets.” --- ### sstk_t2i **Path:** `azure-us-external://sstk/processed/` \| **Weight:** 0.15 \| **Captions:** `api_captions`, `meta_aes_df_scores` \| **Filters:** NSFW\<0.4, IS_NSFW==“no” A large-scale, high-quality dataset sourced from Shutterstock’s commercial stock photography library. 3. *(og)* “Cozy cabin by the lake with autumn trees.”
4. *(detailed)* “A professional product photograph of a luxury watch on a marble surface, with dramatic side lighting creating defined shadows.”
5. *(cube)* “Replace the background with a mountain landscape and add warm sunset lighting.” --- ### carrot_augs **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/zip/carrot6M` \| **Size:** \~6M images \| **Captions:** Auto-generated by `ImageAugmentationCaptionGenerator` Augmentation-reversal dataset. Target images are programmatically degraded (blur, JPEG, grain, contrast/saturation/brightness, pixelation), and captions describe the reversal task. 10% swap probability flips direction. **Sample Prompts:**
1. “Remove the blur from this image.”
2. “Enhance the quality of this compressed image.”
3. “Remove the film grain and noise from the photograph.”
4. “Reduce the contrast and desaturate the image slightly.”
5. “Sharpen and depixelate this image to restore detail.” --- ### carrot_t2i **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/zip/carrot6M` \| **Captions:** CogVLM2: `detailed` (35%), `long` (25%), `short` (20%), `word` (20%) T2I variant of Carrot 6M – single images only (no pairs). Favors detailed CogVLM2 descriptions while including terse prompts. **Sample Prompts:**
1. *(detailed)* “A sunlit meadow filled with wildflowers stretching toward distant rolling hills, with a dirt path winding through the center, golden hour photography.”
2. *(long)* “Colorful wildflower meadow with rolling hills and a winding path at golden hour.”
3. *(short)* “Wildflower meadow at sunset.”
4. *(word)* “meadow flowers sunset”
5. *(detailed)* “A close-up portrait of an elderly craftsman in his workshop, hands weathered from years of woodworking, surrounded by hand tools.” --- ### doppel **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/doppel` \| **Tars:** `good_tars` \| **Captions:** 5 levels (same as jawbreaker_v3) I2I paired dataset with visually related images for subtle transformations or style-consistent generation. Quality-filtered subset (“good_” prefix). **Sample Prompts:**
1. *(long)* “Transform this portrait to match the lighting and color grading of the reference, maintaining identity while adjusting to a warmer, cinematic tone.”
2. *(medium)* “Match the style and mood of the reference image.”
3. *(short)* “Copy this style.”
4. *(very_short)* “Style match.”
5. *(human)* “Make this look like the other photo.” --- ### discord_winners **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/bagel_discord_dpo_with_prompts_and_cherries_v2/zip/` \| **Captions:** `prompt` from JSON Community-curated DPO. Four output candidates per input, scored by Discord upvotes. Highest-voted image becomes training target. “Best-of-N” signal from community preferences. **Sample Prompts:**
1. “Make this photo look like a watercolor painting.”
2. “Remove the background and place the subject in a forest.”
3. “Turn this selfie into a professional headshot.”
4. “Add dramatic lighting to this portrait.”
5. “Change the season from summer to winter in this landscape.” --- ### non_zip_discord_winners_i2i / non_zip_discord_winners_t2i **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/bagel_discord_data/data/` \| **Tars:** `meta_2025_05_13_v3_i2i` / `meta_2025_05_13_v3_t2i` Non-zipped variants of Discord winners. I2I variant requires input images; T2I variant uses only output candidates. **Sample Prompts (I2I):**
1. “Transform this image into a cyberpunk aesthetic.”
2. “Age the subject by 30 years realistically.”
3. “Change the art style to Studio Ghibli anime.”
4. “Replace the sky with an aurora borealis.”
5. “Make this photo look like it was taken in the 1920s.” **Sample Prompts (T2I):**
1. “A majestic phoenix rising from golden flames against a starry night sky.”
2. “Photorealistic portrait of a warrior elf with silver armor in a mystical forest.”
3. “A cozy coffee shop interior on a rainy evening, warm lighting, steam from cups.”
4. “Underwater city with bioluminescent buildings and marine life.”
5. “A steampunk clockwork dragon perched on Big Ben.” --- ### gummie_cola **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/gummie_cola` \| **Captions:** `prompt` from JSON I2I paired dataset with simple prompt-based editing instructions. Default weight 0.0. **Sample Prompts:**
1. “Change the background to a tropical beach.”
2. “Apply a vintage film filter to the photograph.”
3. “Transform this sketch into a photorealistic image.”
4. “Add snow to the ground and make the trees bare.”
5. “Brighten the image and enhance the colors.” --- ### signon **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/signon/` \| **Captions:** 5 levels (same as jawbreaker_v3) Sign and text generation dataset. Improves text generation on signs, labels, banners, and similar surfaces. **Sample Prompts:**
1. *(long)* “Replace the text on the storefront sign with ‘Grand Opening Sale’, keeping the same font style and neon illumination.”
2. *(medium)* “Change the sign text to ‘Grand Opening Sale’.”
3. *(short)* “Update the sign text.”
4. *(very_short)* “Edit text.”
5. *(human)* “Can you change what the sign says to something about a grand opening?” --- ### ganger **Path:** `/blob/raw/data/ganger` \| **Tars:** `good_samples_tars_fixed` \| **Captions:** `cube.instruction.txt` I2I paired dataset with Cube VLM structured editing instructions. Quality-filtered and bug-fixed. Derived from `objectum_shapes`. **Sample Prompts:**
1. “Remove the object in the center of the image and fill with the surrounding background texture.”
2. “Change the material of the furniture from wood to brushed metal.”
3. “Add a reflection of the object on the surface below it.”
4. “Modify the shape of the vase to be taller and more narrow.”
5. “Replace the pattern on the fabric with a floral design while preserving the folds and wrinkles.” "}

title: Large-scale Video Data Project
content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Large-scale Video Data Project","url":"https://www.notion.so/2b1c370222d58046a04dea40a9b77d26","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2b1c370222d58046a04dea40a9b77d26 as of 2025-11-22T02:06:56.522Z: {"title":"Large-scale Video Data Project"} We are in the process of acquiring O(100 PiB) of video data - There is 1.4BN videos available from wyndlabs. We need to decide how much we would like to acquire. I think we should do some cost modeling for different dataset scales and do the maximum we are comfortable spending. - is also acquiring a large common crawl video set. Action items: - PR and link current Captioning workflow - Next step: Can we optimize speed? - reaching out to storage companies (don’t exactly remember the names) Questions to answer: - Where are we storing the data? - To answer this we first need to figure out where we want to train with this data. My assumption is ideally everywhere. - How does transfer work? - How are we storing the data? - For Azure Blob storage a flat structure is better. - Processing of the data to prepare for training - Captioning - How long does it take given how many GPUs? - Do we have the final setup that we are confident with? In the past we have wasted quite a bit compute on re-captioning. - Clipping - How long does it take given how many CPUs? - Other processing steps: embedding computation, motion scores - How long does it take give how many GPUs - Training - Will the amount of training compute we have available be a factor in the size of our datasets. title: Lead Scoring Guide
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Lead Scoring Guide","url":"https://www.notion.so/343c370222d581598bf2e0c9ec6fdea4","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/343c370222d581598bf2e0c9ec6fdea4 as of 2026-04-17T10:13:12.897Z: {"Verification":"verified","title":"Lead Scoring Guide"} ## What is lead scoring? Every inbound lead from the BFL contact form is automatically scored out of 11 points. The score tells you how likely a lead is to convert to a paying customer. Anything 4 points or above is flagged as sales-ready and should be followed up. Any lead selecting enterprise as their licensing tier is also flagged regardless of score. --- ## How points are assigned Each lead is scored on five things: ### Image generation volume How many images they expect to generate per month.
Answer Points
1M+ 4
100,000–1,000,000 2
10,000–100,000 1
0–10,000 or no idea 0
### Company size Enriched automatically via Clay.
Employees Points
1,000+ 3
251–1,000 2
1–250 1
### Job title
Title Points
C-suite, VP, Director, Head of 1
Everything else 0
### What they're interested in
Selection Points
API or flux-license 1
Other 0
### Use case description A Clay formula field checks for "flux" or "lora" in the free-text use case field. No AI credits used.
Content Points
Mentions "flux" or "lora" (case insensitive) 2
Neither mentioned or field is empty 0
If someone names a specific model, they've already tested it — high buying intent. --- ## Who to prioritise Three types of leads are always worth a conversation: **High volume users** — anyone selecting 1M+ image generations scores 4 points from that field alone. These are likely platform or enterprise customers. **Large enterprises with unknown volume** — a 1,000+ employee company with an exec title and API or licensing interest will score 4+ even if they selected "I have no idea" on image volume. **Leads mentioning a specific model or LoRA** — even a small company with a low image gen estimate is worth a look if they've named a specific model. It means they've already built something with it. --- ## How leads get to Clay Leads flow from Attio to Clay via a dedicated view called **"Lead Enrichment (Clay Integration Do Not Edit)"** on the People object. This view filters to only show: - Leads where `Lead Source` = `contact-sales-form` - Emails that are not personal addresses (no gmail, hotmail, icloud, yahoo, or outlook) This means only genuine inbound form submissions with company emails are sent for enrichment. Do not modify this view. --- ## Scoring is a starting point, not a final answer The score is a starting point for triage, not the final word. Always read the use case description before reaching out. Lead scoring is an iterative process, so feedback is welcome on how we can further improve. For the first few weeks, leads scoring 1–3 will also be compiled into a weekly digest for a quick team review, to make sure nothing good is being missed while the formula is being calibrated. Geography and industry scoring will be added in a future update. "}

title: Legal / commercial / backend ops
content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Legal / commercial / backend ops","url":"https://www.notion.so/256c370222d580afaa86d74eb7c65c15","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/256c370222d580afaa86d74eb7c65c15 as of 2025-10-14T16:01:53.120Z: {"title":"Legal / commercial / backend ops"} This page is meant to capture the collaboration between legal, commercial and backend when it comes to capture important agreement details. Here is the Google sheet capturing the information: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1am5Q-abUWcXmmjzk3etTAg7na5VuF66sg4KSWQwVPPY/edit?gid=0#gid=0](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1am5Q-abUWcXmmjzk3etTAg7na5VuF66sg4KSWQwVPPY/edit?gid=0#gid=0) ## Legal Agreement Process Objective: Set up an efficient process enabling a smooth and fast collaboration between GTM teams and legal - progress is tracked in Slack and Attio Reminder: This is NOT a process where GTM throws an agreement over the fence to legal. We need to collaborate to reduce back and forth and increase deal speed ALWAYS take our agreements, NEVER take the customers papers ## Largest blockers Jan - Sep 25 have been - Lack of human resources ✅ - Communication gaps with external lawyers 🚧 - GTM team legal enablement & knowledge 🚧 ## Legal Agreement Workflow 1. **Pre-Screening**. For certain deals, e.g. with Enterprises, it makes sense to discuss sensitive topics before sending over an agreement from our end. A [Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1EkuIhQ3LHVsT1N2bwmZWFT6d7-eNDKg6?usp=drive_link) should be in place prior to discussion of these topics. These topics are: - can we use their data to train our models? - do they need 0-data-retention? - can we ask to use their logo or would this trigger a lengthy approval process? Note: in general we should always push for logo, potentially give more discount, but we should not slow down a deal unnecessarily - Indemnification, see - If you can get all necessary info to fill out the Order Form beforehand you can already insert it for them to check - **By surfacing these topics early we can avoid deal breakers and delays later during the legal phase of the negotiation** 2. **Adjust and send Template**. Business team chooses the right template from ([drive.google.com](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1nyW6pUruVWYqBv81Q8wfxN6P4n2qMyN0)), creates a copy for the specific customer in the customer’s dedicated Google Drive folder in the sub-folder “legal drafts” - Decide what template is needed - is an Order Form enough or do we need a full agreement? —\> Always try to avoid setting up a full API Enterprise Agreement. Some customers, e.g. startups, are totally fine with Order Forms. - Decide if Black Forest Labs Inc. or BFL GmbH should be used for the agreement - If non-standard deviations are needed, e.g. zero-data-retention, no training, non-standard indemnification level, **please consult with legal via **[**Slack**](slackChannel://black-forest-labs.slack.com/C08KH2QGF45) - Once our draft is complete in the Google document (note: be careful to remove any Internal-only comments), download and send over to customer as Word Document so they can do their review 3. **Negotiate agreement**. You receive a redlined response from the customer - Update the status of the deal to “legal” in the CRM in case it makes sense (e.g. you are not mainly working on technical challenges and legal is happening on the side) - **Once you receive their legal redlines, make sure to read them, check their comments and leave comments for your legal team in the document to give them more context. Summarize how you have understood the redlines and your thoughts.** - Please click on “request form” in the [Slack channel ](slackChannel://black-forest-labs.slack.com/C08KH2QGF45)[**bfl-help-commercial-legal-external**](slackChannel://black-forest-labs.slack.com/C08KH2QGF45)** **and fill out the details - will assign a member of the legal team to take care of the issue - a discussion in the document and/or on the Slack request might happen - Once redlines are complete from our end, Business team member sends back the redline to the counterparty - Repeat this process until the parties have agreed (or a party walked away from the deal - we had to do this a couple of times because of extreme indemnification requirements that a deal would not justify) 4. **\[If needed: schedule negotiation call\] **If needed a legal call can be set up - this should be avoided for small and medium sized deals 5. **Update document status**. Once legal review is done, update the status in Slack 6. **Save executed agreement**. When the agreement is signed, please upload the pdf to **both,** 1. a newly created “Contracts” folder in the respective Customer/Partnership folder **and** 2. the [Sales&Marketing/Sales/Customers/ZZ_Executed Agreements (unsorted)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1n1wCWt3OKt85YpRnsDJ43JwV6gU1ciqf?usp=drive_link) folder or the [Sales&Marketing/Partnerships/ZZ_Executed Partnership Agreements (unsorted)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1LR_A_viniYuY2yZ4_p9eF9vIstjMDFDX?usp=drive_link) folder. (This ensures that the agreements are reflected in the [Agreement Database](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1_EM_z6LHWPMwibWFDGbeZX2PFYaDSh-x/edit?usp=drive_link&ouid=117009868738180578161&rtpof=true&sd=true) maintained by the legal team.) ## Core API Agreement Information - **Developer Legal Name** - The API customer's official entity name - **Company Legal Name **- Black Forest Labs Inc. or BFL GmbH - **Developer ID/API Key** - Unique identifier for API access - **Effective Date** - When the agreement begins - **Term Type** - Initial term length (e.g., 1 year) and renewal periods - **Termination Notice Period** - Required notice period (e.g., 60 days) ## Model Access & Pricing - EXCLUDED FOR NOW - **Flux AI Model Versions** - Which models they have access to: - FLUX.1 \[pro\] - FLUX1.1 \[pro\] / Ultra / Raw - FLUX1.1 \[pro\] Finetuning - FLUX Tools \[pro\] (Fill, Canny, Depth, Redux) - FLUX.1 Kontext \[pro\] / \[max\] - **Pricing Structure**: - Cost per image generated (inference costs) - Minimum monthly commit (if applicable) - Whether fees are usage-based or include minimum guarantees ## Usage & Compliance Tracking - **Inference Cluster Location** - Global, United States, or Sweden - **Training Status** - Per Section 2.9, whether they've opted out of having their inputs/outputs used for model training - **Rate Limits** - Current API rate limits agreed upon - **SLAs** - Standard of modified ## Data Processing & Privacy - **DPA Status** - Whether Data Processing Agreement is in place - **Data Retention Preferences**: - Outputs retention - no retention or 5 hours - Input prompts retention - no retention or 0 hours - **Indemnification Type** - Which indemnification option was selected: - No indemnification - Patent infringement only - Patent + DPA breach - Patent + DPA + Outputs ## Additional Tracking Fields - **Billing Contact** - For invoicing - **Technical Contact** - For API support - **Auto-Renewal Status** - Whether agreement auto-renews - **Renewal data** - For GTM team to reach out again "}
