{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"📈 Sales Weekly","url":"https://www.notion.so/309c370222d5816ba3c8c6a8fcb14564","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/309c370222d5816ba3c8c6a8fcb14564 as of 2026-03-31T15:48:08.900Z: {"title":"Sales Weekly"} **Cadence:** Weekly, 30 min \| **Attendees:** Seb, Sam, Anthony **Purpose:** The Sales Weekly is the team's one structured pipeline call per week. It exists to keep us honest on revenue, surface risks early, drive decisions on deals, and hold each other accountable on goals. This is not a status update — it's a working session. Come prepared, leave with actions. --- # Agenda
# Section Time Purpose
1 Rev Snapshot 5 min Where are we against \$43M ARR target? Key movers up and down.
2 Closing the gap 5 min What can we do?
3 Pipe Health + Leads 3 min Quick scan: overdue deals, stale deals, lead volume and triage status.
4 Top Deals 7 min Only deals that need a decision — at risk, blocked, or closing soon.
5 Signals 0-2 min Only if someone has something worth sharing. Not a standing section.
6 Key Initiatives 5 min Strategic work: closed-weights, open-weights/FDE, enterprise PG, RevOps. What moved, what's stuck.
7 Decisions & Next Steps 3 min What we decided, who owns what, by when.
--- # Prep **Before each call, everyone comes with:** Your top 2-3 deals — where they stand, next step, where you need help. Your goal tracking status — are you on pace, behind, or blocked? One signal or pattern from your conversations that week. Any blockers the team should know about. --- # Q1 Goals
Owner Goal Metric
Team \$43M avg API ARR Monthly API revenue annualized
Team \$3M net new ARR ARR delta from Q1 start to Q1 end
--- # Meeting Notes Feb 18, 2026 Sales Weekly — Mar 3 2026 Q1 2026 — Revenue Recap "}

title: Senior Partnerships Manager
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"🤝🏼 Senior Partnerships Manager","url":"https://www.notion.so/1f1c370222d580ccbfb2d2b821187466","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/1f1c370222d580ccbfb2d2b821187466 as of 2026-04-15T10:06:44.141Z: {"title":"Senior Partnerships Manager"} We’re currently asking all roles to work from one of the office locations (i.e. Freiburg or SF). Please mention that upfront if people ask.
For additional context: For exceptional candidates we can be flexible with the location a hire is living in once they commit to coming 3 days a week into one of the offices. However, please don’t bring this up in the convo with a candidate without checking back with Andi before. ***Deadline: Wed, 11th of Feb*** - [ ] Create lightweight candidate prep package (***will finalize when we have aligned on the interview outline + case study***) - [x] Scorecard: add what meets expectations, what not —\> add technical questions in the beginning! - [x] Revamp sales case-study - potentially several case-studies by role and seniority? More context, more guardrails? For more mid-level simpler case-study. Idea from offsite: reseller would be good case-study ## What are we looking for --- The ideal candidate for this role combines high autonomy with deep industry expertise and expert-level negotiation skills. Below are the core qualities and what they look like in practice.
Quality What this looks like
**High Autonomy/
Agency** **Operator**		 • Ability to move fast and aggressively, and to pivot when needed. Comfortable operating with minimal oversight in a startup environment.
• Proactively identifies opportunities and acts on them without waiting for direction.
**Deep Industry Expertise** • Experience in the generative AI space, particularly text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-image (t2i/t2v/i2i)
• Profound technical knowledge involving: 1) generative AI for media, or 2) cloud computing, particularly on the GPU side
• Direct experience working with model resellers and API inference providers (e.g. Fal, Replicate, Together AI)
**Deal Execution / Expert Negotiator** • Ability to negotiate complex deals with the globally largest B2B / API businesses, including bi-directional deals involving compute and data
• Knowledge of the dynamics of open source business models and monetization strategies
• Understanding of reseller economics, rev-share structures, and competitive positioning against models like Nano Banana (Google) and GPT Image (OpenAI)
## Interview Process --- Each stage of the interview process is designed to evaluate a distinct set of competencies. The objectives below outline what each interviewer should focus on gauging throughout their conversation.
Phase Description Objective
Step 0 Referral Only Align on role, expectations, responsibilities, and BFL as a company. Conduct first culture check and verify that the org setup works for the candidate.
Step 1
 Recruiter Screen Gauge general fit, interest in the role, salary expectations, location/hybrid requirements, and availability. Surface any immediate disqualifiers.
Step 2
 Peer Interview (Partnerships) Gauge 1) level of autonomy and ability to work in ambiguity, 2) strategic thinking and ability to understand complex orgs/concepts, and 3) depth of experience with large, complex partnership deals and ability to navigate multi-stakeholder negotiations.
Step 3
 Peer Interview (Partnerships) Gauge 1) rigor of territory and pipeline management, including segmentation, forecasting, and tracking, 2) commercial operations mindset, specifically the ability to identify, automate, and scale repeatable sales processes, and 3) technical depth sufficient for partnerships (generative AI, GPU infrastructure, model inference),
Step 4
 Executive Interview Gauge 1) overall BFL culture fit and startup DNA, 2) knowledge of the competitive landscape and open source business model dynamics, and 3) ability to navigate complex legal/commercial negotiations (e.g. indemnification, 3P IP rights).
Step 5 Onsite & Case Study Gauge real-world problem-solving ability through a reseller strategy case study. Evaluate the candidate’s ability to synthesize market data into an actionable growth plan, present and defend strategic recommendations under pressure, and demonstrate commercial creativity for BFL’s unique positioning.
### Interviewer Question Bank --- All questions follow the STARR framework: Situation, Task, Action, Result, Reflection. Each section includes the core question, drill-down prompts, and what to listen for.
**Step 2 - Peer Interview: Strategic Thinking & Deal Complexity** *Interviewer: \[Interviewer Name\]  \|  Duration: 45 min  \|  Focus: autonomy, strategic thinking, complex deal navigation* **Large, Complex Strategic Deal Experience (30%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Tell me about the most complex deal you’ve worked on, and what made it complicated? How did the incentives of you and the partner overlap? How did they differ? Were there competing models (e.g. from Google, OpenAI) in the picture?
**T** What specific objectives were you trying to achieve, and what was your role specifically? What strategic trade-offs were in consideration? E.g. short-term revenue vs. long-term exclusivity, rev-share vs. flat fee?
**A** Were there internal stakeholders who were hesitant? Why? What did you do to change their mind? How did you research the partner’s business strategy? How did you create and keep urgency? What data or frameworks did you use to build the business case?
**R** What was the result? (Relevant metrics, longevity of deal, partner management handoff.) Was the deal renewed? Were there differing opinions of success internally? Who decided?
**R** If you ran the same deal today, what would you do differently? Look for concrete, not generic, improvements. Do they reference lessons applicable to BFL’s reseller dynamics?
**Ability to Work Through Ambiguity (25%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Tell me about a time when you pitched a deal that was novel or untested in the company. What was the inspiration, and how did you go about creating the case? Who were the stakeholders? What was the competitive pressure? How was the initiative resourced?
**T** How did you navigate the org to get approval and resourcing? Was anyone opposed? How did you get it on the roadmap? Was there a parallel between this and operating at a startup like BFL?
**A** How did you approach the partner? How did you align timing and incentives? What research did you do on the partner’s business strategy? What tools or frameworks did you use?
**R** What were the concrete outcomes? Revenue impact? New market opened? Internal process established?
**R** What would you do differently next time? Does the candidate show genuine self-awareness?
**—** Bonus: What is the least-favourite part of your job, and how do you manage it? Reveals self-awareness, honesty, and resilience. Red flag if they say “nothing.”
**Reasoning & Judgement (20%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Tell me about a time when you deliberately lost a deal or walked away. Why, and what was your strategy? What signals told you to walk? Was it a rev-share issue, misaligned incentives, or competitive risk?
**T** What was the initial rationale for the deal? When did you realize it wasn’t going to work out? How did they weigh short-term revenue against long-term strategic positioning?
**A** How did you convince internal management? How did you communicate the decision to the partner? Did they propose an alternative? How did they protect the relationship even while walking away?
**R** What were the downstream effects? Pipeline metrics at day 30/60/90? Did walking away create space for a better deal? Was the relationship salvaged later?
**R** Looking back, what would you prioritize differently in month 1? Look for lessons about deal qualification, partner selection criteria, or rev-share thresholds.
**BFL-Specific Discussion Questions ** *Use these as open-ended discussion prompts toward the end of the interview* 1. What would you consider the biggest challenges that Black Forest Labs might be facing in our effort to build high-value and sustainable partnerships? 2. How do you build champions inside an account, especially in complex environments where multiple teams (product, engineering, procurement) have a say? 3. What is your experience with model resellers or API inference platforms? How would you think about structuring those relationships? **Step 2 Scorecard**
**Competency** **Does Not Meet** **Meets Expectations** **Exceeds Expectations**
**Autonomy & Ambiguity** Needs clear direction and structure to operate. Examples rely on well-defined playbooks or heavy manager involvement. Uncomfortable with undefined problems. Can describe situations where they operated independently with incomplete information. Took reasonable initiative but typically within established frameworks. Proactively identified and pursued opportunities with no playbook. Built the framework themselves. Thrives in chaos and can point to outcomes that resulted directly from their independent judgment.
**Strategic Thinking** Tactical and transactional in approach. Struggles to explain the “why” behind deal structures. Cannot articulate trade-offs or connect deals to broader business strategy. Understands the strategic rationale behind deals. Can explain trade-offs (short-term vs. long-term, rev-share vs. flat fee) and how deal terms connect to company objectives. Thinks multiple moves ahead. Proactively identifies how a deal reshapes the competitive landscape or creates leverage for future partnerships. Can map partner incentives to BFL’s strategic position unprompted.
**Complex Deal Navigation** Deals cited are simple, single-stakeholder, or primarily inbound. Cannot describe navigating competing internal interests or multi-party negotiations. Has closed deals involving multiple stakeholders, competing priorities, and meaningful commercial complexity. Can walk through how they managed the process end-to-end. Has led transformative, multi-million-dollar or multi-party deals with competing incentives. Built consensus across skeptical stakeholders. Can articulate how they created urgency and aligned parties with fundamentally different goals.
**Step 3 - Peer Interview: Pipeline Management, Commercial Operations & Technical Depth** *Interviewer: \[Interviewer Name\]  \|  Duration: 30 min  \|  Focus: territory management, scaling operations, technical depth for partnerships* **Partner Pipeline Management (35%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Walk me through your last managed set of partners: the strategy you created, how you executed it, and results. Details on: # of partners, regions, verticals, company size (ENT/SMB), novel deal vs. existing framework. What were the business or technical models involved? SaaS, licenses, AI models, compute?
**T** Did you have a quota or business KPI? What baseline revenue were you coming from? Other KPIs (upselling, closing large commitments)? Were there specific “must-win” partners? How were mutual goals set?
**A** How did you prioritize partners to pursue? What were specific metrics tracked for the deals? Forecasting approach (bottoms-up/top-down)? How did you handle the long-tail? Did you create a playbook?
**R** How did you perform against goals? What were the key drivers? Was it riding the wave or specific initiatives? Tracking cadence (monthly, quarterly, yearly)?
**R** In hindsight, what would you do differently? What key learnings would you apply to BFL? Do they reference anything relevant to BFL’s model (API-first, open source, reseller distribution)?
**Commercial Operations & Scaling (30%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Describe a time you automated or scaled a manual partnership step or bottleneck that had a big impact. What was your role? How long did you own this? Why did nobody else tackle this? How complex was the problem?
**T** What efficiency, quality, or cost goal did you set? Was there a goal from management? Time or cost saved? How did this feed into overall goals?
**A** Which tools, playbooks, or integrations did you build or launch? What was the technical lift? Did you involve engineering or do it yourself?
**R** KPIs proving success: hours saved, adoption rate, error reduction. How was this rated by stakeholders (customers, partners, your manager)?
**R** What would you have done differently? How did you share learnings with the org? Did this become an org-wide standard?
**Technical Depth for Partnerships (35%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Give me an example of a partnership deal where you had to learn a new technical concept from scratch and the impact it had on the business., e.g. model inference, GPU pricing, cloud infrastructure How much were you in contact with that concept beforehand? What was the technical complexity?
**T** What technical problem or hypothesis were you trying to solve? How did you define success? Was it driven by a competitive trigger, a market shift, or partner/customer feedback?
**A** Walk me through how you ramped up technically: research sources, frameworks, engineers or experts you tapped. How did you collaborate with engineering or product teams? Were there implications on pricing, architecture, or product roadmap?
**R** What changed after you applied that technical insight? Give me KPIs. Internal influence on pricing, packaging, infrastructure decisions, or go-to-market?
**R** How do these technical learnings guide your approach to new partnerships? What would you do differently? What was the single thing with the biggest impact? Do they reference concepts relevant to BFL (inference costs, GPU allocation, model hosting)?
**Technical Depth Discussion Questions (Interviewer 2)** 1. Can you explain, at a high level, how a text-to-image model like FLUX generates an image from a prompt? Walk me through it as you would explain it to a technical buyer. 2. What’s the difference between a customer using BFL’s hosted API vs. a reseller who self-hosts our model on their own GPUs? What are the trade-offs for the customer? 3. If a partner tells you their inference costs on FLUX are too high compared to a competing model, how would you diagnose and respond to that? 4. What do you understand about the economics of GPU inference? How does GPU type, batch size, or optimization affect cost per image? **Step 3 Scorecard**
**Competency** **Does Not Meet** **Meets Expectations** **Exceeds Expectations**
**Territory & Pipeline Management** Cannot clearly articulate their territory strategy or how they prioritized accounts. Reactive rather than systematic. No clear metrics or forecasting discipline. Pipeline management sounds ad-hoc. Had a structured territory plan with clear segmentation logic. Tracked pipeline metrics consistently (stage, value, velocity). Used a forecasting methodology (bottoms-up or top-down) and can explain how they hit quota. Built the territory playbook from scratch or significantly improved an inherited one. Data-driven segmentation with clear ROI logic. Created forecasting models that leadership relied on. Consistently over-quota with attributable initiatives, not just market tailwinds.
**Commercial Operations & Scaling** No examples of identifying and fixing process bottlenecks. Relies entirely on manual effort. Does not think about repeatability or scalability of their work. Can point to at least one process they automated or scaled. Understands the value of playbooks and tooling. Measurable impact (time saved, error reduction, adoption). Has a pattern of building scalable systems: playbooks, self-serve tools, CRM automations, or partner enablement programs that others adopted. Thinks like an operator, not just a seller. Impact was org-wide, not just personal.
**Technical Depth** Cannot explain generative AI concepts at a level suitable for partner conversations. Confuses basic terminology (inference vs. training, API vs. model hosting). Would need significant technical ramp-up. Can explain t2i model inference, the difference between hosted vs. self-hosted, and basic GPU economics at a level sufficient to have credible partner conversations. Understands the BFL API vs. reseller distinction. Deep technical fluency: can discuss inference optimization, GPU cost structures, model fine-tuning, and latency trade-offs confidently. Has used this knowledge to structure better deals or win technical buyers. Could hold their own with an engineering counterpart at a partner.
**Step 4 - Executive Interview: Culture Fit, Competitive Landscape & Legal** *Interviewer: \[Interviewer Name\]  \|  Duration: 30** min**  \|  Focus: BFL culture fit, startup DNA, competitive landscape, open source dynamics, legal/commercial negotiations* **Culture Fit & Startup DNA (35%)**
**Phase** **Core Question** **Drill-down Prompts**
**S** Describe an unusual initiative you led completely outside your job scope to hit a big goal. What was the context? Why did nobody else do it? How does this reflect how you’d operate at a 50-person startup like BFL?
**T** What outcome did you aim for and why was it mission-critical? How did you frame the urgency? Was this sanctioned from above or did you just run with it?
**A** Which resources did you mobilize yourself — budget, people, tools? Did you have to build consensus or just act? How do you decide when to ask for permission vs. forgiveness?
**R** Measurable results: revenue, PR, community, or recruiting impact? What lasting asset came out of it (playbook, ritual, process)?
**R** What would you have done differently? What did this reveal about how you operate vs. a traditional enterprise seller?
**Culture Fit Discussion Prompts** 1. Core: Why are you excited about joining BFL vs. other generative AI companies? 1. Listen for: Specificity about BFL’s FLUX models, open-source philosophy, and unique positioning. Generic “I love AI” answers are a red flag. 2. Core: What are your favorite tools in the image generation space and why? 1. Listen for: Genuine enthusiasm and hands-on familiarity (Midjourney, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, FLUX). Do they use these tools personally? **Competitive Landscape & Open Source Business Model (35%)** 1. Core: From your perception of BFL, how would you describe our business model? 1. Listen for: Understanding of the open-source-plus-API model, reseller distribution, and how BFL monetizes. Bonus: awareness of the tension between open weights and commercial licensing. 2. Core: What do you think makes BFL special and different from other media generation companies or big tech firms that offer image/video generation? 1. Listen for: Open source community, model quality, speed of innovation, independence from big tech. 3. Core: From your experience, what might be the general challenges regarding the business model and legal risks for an open source model provider like BFL? 1. Probe: Business model: How to monetize open source effectively. Legal: Copyright considerations (Stability AI case precedent), controlling illegal content generation with open models. **Legal & Commercial Negotiations (30%)** 1. Core: Walk me through a negotiation where indemnification was a sticking point. How did you resolve it? 1. Context: At BFL, counterparties frequently ask for full indemnity including third-party rights; BFL typically only provides patent rights. 1. Probe: What are the challenges and risks especially around third-party rights? How would you resolve this with a large enterprise customer? 1. Listen for: Understanding of IP risk in generative AI, practical frameworks for tiered indemnification, creative solutions (caps, carve-outs, insurance). 2. Core: Tell me about a time you had to push back on a partner’s legal or commercial demands. How did you protect the company’s interests without killing the deal? 1. Listen for: Maturity in balancing commercial pressure with risk management. Are they comfortable saying no? Do they propose creative alternatives? **Step 4 Scorecard**
**Competency** **Does Not Meet** **Meets Expectations** **Exceeds Expectations**
**Culture Fit & Startup DNA** Primarily enterprise-minded: expects established processes, large support teams, and clear swim lanes. No examples of going outside their job scope. Risk-averse and consensus-driven in a way that would slow down a 50-person startup. Shows comfort operating in a lean environment. Has examples of taking initiative beyond their defined role. Motivated by BFL’s mission and understands the pace required at a startup. Has a track record of building things from zero in fast-moving environments. Permission-vs-forgiveness mentality with good judgment. Genuinely energized by BFL’s open source approach and FLUX specifically — not just “AI is exciting.” Has used the tools personally.
**Competitive Landscape & Open Source** Surface-level knowledge of generative AI market. Cannot differentiate BFL from competitors. Does not understand the tension between open weights and commercial monetization. Generic answers about “open source being great.” Understands BFL’s positioning vs. big tech (Google, OpenAI) and other open source players. Can articulate the open-source-plus-API business model and its core challenges (monetization, content control, copyright). Nuanced understanding of the competitive landscape including specific model comparisons (FLUX vs. Imagen vs. DALL-E). Can discuss open source monetization strategies with depth (dual licensing, API premium, fine-tuning moats). Aware of legal precedents (Stability AI case) and their implications for BFL.
**Legal & Commercial Negotiations** No experience with complex commercial negotiations. Cannot discuss indemnification, IP risk, or third-party rights beyond surface level. Would need legal hand-holding on every deal. Has navigated commercial negotiations involving indemnification, liability caps, or IP clauses. Understands the concept of third-party IP risk in generative AI. Can push back on partner demands while maintaining the relationship. Has personally structured creative legal/commercial solutions (tiered indemnification, carve-outs, liability caps, insurance mechanisms) for complex deals. Deeply understands generative AI IP risk. Can balance commercial pressure with risk management independently and propose novel frameworks.
### Case Study (Reseller Version) --- Provide this brief to the candidate during the onsite. The candidate should prepare a 20–25 minute presentation, followed by 20–25 minutes of Q&A. ### **Case Study Brief: Reseller Channel Strategy for Black Forest Labs** **Background** Black Forest Labs (BFL) is the creator of FLUX, a family of state-of-the-art generative AI models for image and video generation. BFL distributes its models through primary channels: 1. **Direct via BFL API (api.bfl.ml) or Open Weights**: BFL’s own hosted API, where customers pay BFL directly for inference, or direct access to Model Weights with commercial licensing options. 2. **API Access via Reseller / Inference Partners**: Third-party platforms (e.g. Fal, Replicate, and other large API resellers) that either re-sell BFL’s API or host FLUX models on their own infrastructure and sell access via their own APIs. **
The Problem** The original hypothesis was that reseller platforms would drive traffic to BFL’s own API (i.e., discovering our APIs through a reseller platform and switching to direct integration). This has not materialized. Instead, BFL frequently competes directly with its own resellers on deals and customers stay permanently at resellers instead of changing to the BFL API. The CEO has set a target of \$500K monthly image generation revenue within 6 months (up from \$280K today) and wants a clear channel strategy to get there. **Current Channel Economics (Monthly Averages, Last Quarter)**
**Channel** **Monthly Images** **Price / Image** **BFL Rev / Image** **BFL Monthly Rev** **Gross Margin**
**BFL Direct API** 1.2M \$0.14 \$0.14 \$168K \~62%
**Reseller A (re-sells BFL API)** 2.8M \$0.12 \$0.06 \$168K \~28%
**Reseller B (self-hosts FLUX, with own API)** 4.5M \$0.10 \$0.03\* \$135K \~100%†
**Long-tail resellers (mixed)** 1.1M varies \~\$0.06 \$66K varies
*\*Reseller B pays a flat royalty of \$0.03/image under an older agreement. BFL bears no infrastructure cost for self-hosted resellers (royalty is pure margin), but the royalty rate is well below the \$0.06 minimum in newer contracts.* **Total monthly BFL revenue:** \~\$537K gross / \~\$280K net (after infrastructure costs on direct API and Reseller A channels). **Target:** \$500K net monthly revenue within 6 months. **Additional Context** 1. **Competitive dynamic: **Resellers bundle FLUX alongside competing models (e.g. NanoBanana from Google, GPT Image from OpenAI), giving customers easy access to alternatives and reducing BFL’s leverage. In the last quarter, Reseller B’s FLUX volume declined 12% month-over-month as they began promoting a competing model more prominently. 2. **Customer behavior: **A recent survey of 50 reseller customers found: 42% chose the reseller because they already used the platform for other models, 28% cited better developer tooling/documentation, 18% cited multi-model access as a key requirement, and 12% said they didn’t know BFL had a direct API. 3. **Infrastructure:** BFL’s direct API infrastructure costs \~\$0.053/image at current scale. The engineering team estimates that cost drops to \~\$0.04/image at 3x current volume due to GPU utilization improvements. **Your Assignment** You have been hired as BFL’s Senior Partnerships Manager. The CEO has asked you to develop a 90-day reseller channel strategy to reach \$500K net monthly revenue. Prepare a presentation that addresses the following: 1. Diagnosis: Using the data above, what is driving the current channel mix? Why are customers choosing resellers, and which reseller relationships are healthy vs. problematic for BFL? 2. Financial Analysis: Model at least two scenarios for reaching the \$500K net revenue target. Show the volume and revenue-per-image assumptions for each channel. What is the most capital-efficient path to the target? 3. Strategic Options: Present 2–3 strategic options for BFL’s reseller channel. These could range from deepening symbiotic relationships (differentiated tiers, co-selling, exclusivity) to reducing dependency on resellers (competing head-to-head, building direct distribution). For each option, quantify the trade-offs. 4. Recommendation: Which option do you recommend and why? Include a phased 30/60/90-day plan with specific milestones and a revenue build showing how you get from \$280K to \$500K net. 5. Competitive Moat: How would you differentiate BFL’s direct offering against resellers who also host competing models? What can BFL offer that a multi-model platform cannot? 6. Metrics: What KPIs would you track to measure channel health? How would you know early if the strategy is working or if you need to pivot? **Constraints & Assumptions** - BFL has a small but growing partnerships team (2–3 people including yourself). - FLUX models are best-in-class for image generation quality and speed. - BFL’s API is functional but does not yet have feature parity with some reseller platforms on developer tooling, dashboard features, or multi-model access. - Engineering has capacity for one major API/platform improvement per quarter. - You may make additional reasonable assumptions, but state them clearly and show your math. **Format** Prepare a Notion doc or deck (10–15 slides recommended). Present for 20–25 minutes, followed by 20–25 minutes of Q&A with the panel- a total of 45 minutes. **Case Study Evaluation Rubric (Internal Only, Do Not Share with Candidate)**
**Evaluation Criteria** **Strong Signal** **Weak Signal**
**Market Diagnosis** Articulates specific reasons customers prefer resellers (multi-model access, DX, existing billing, latency/region). Shows empathy for customer decision-making. Vague or assumption-based. Doesn’t differentiate between types of resellers (re-sellers vs. self-hosters).
**Strategic Thinking** Presents a spectrum of options with clear trade-offs. Recognizes that “kill all resellers” and “keep status quo” are both insufficient. Proposes nuanced tiering or segmentation. Binary thinking (keep or kill). Doesn’t consider BFL’s leverage, scale constraints, or the value resellers provide in market education.
**Competitive Awareness** Understands that resellers bundling Imagen and GPT Image is a real threat. Proposes specific differentiation for FLUX (quality, speed, open weights, customization, fine-tuning). Ignores competitive bundling. Treats resellers as pure distribution without recognizing they also drive model substitution.
**Quantitative Rigor** Builds a clear revenue model with volume and unit-economics assumptions for each channel. Shows a credible bridge from \$280K to \$500K. Identifies which levers (price, volume, channel mix) have the highest ROI. Ignores the financial data or uses it superficially. No revenue model. Handwaves the \$500K target without showing how the math works. Confuses gross and net revenue.
**Commercial Creativity** Proposes creative commercial structures: tiered rev-share by volume, exclusive early access to new models, co-selling programs, preferred pricing for direct API migration. Only proposes raising or lowering prices. No structural creativity.
**Execution Rigor** 30/60/90-day plan with specific milestones, owner assignments, and decision gates. Identifies quick wins vs. longer bets. Vague timeline. No measurable milestones. Plan depends entirely on things outside BFL’s control.
**Metrics & Measurement** Proposes leading and lagging indicators: direct API conversion rate, reseller-attributed revenue trend, revenue per image (direct vs. reseller), customer NPS by channel. Only tracks top-line revenue. No channel-level attribution or health metrics.
**Presentation & Presence** Clear, structured, executive-ready. Handles Q&A with poise. Defends recommendations with data-driven reasoning while remaining open to challenge. Disorganized. Cannot defend assumptions. Becomes defensive under questioning.
**Suggested Q&A Probes for the Panel** 1. If Fal or Replicate came to you and said they want to renegotiate terms to 15% rev-share, how would you respond? 2. A large enterprise customer tells you they prefer using Replicate because they can also access nano banana in the same API call. How do you win them to BFL direct? 3. How would you handle a situation where one of our top resellers starts actively steering customers toward a competing model? 4. What’s the minimum rev-share you’d accept before you’d recommend pulling a model from a reseller? 5. If you could only do one thing in your first 30 days, what would it be and why? 6. How do you see the reseller landscape evolving over the next 12–18 months as more foundation model providers enter the market? 7. Reseller B’s FLUX volume dropped 12% last month. At what point do you renegotiate the \$0.03 royalty, and what leverage do you have? 8. Looking at the customer survey data, 12% didn’t know BFL had a direct API. How much revenue does that represent, and what would you do about it in the first 30 days? 9. How would you handle the situation where Reseller B starts actively steering customers toward a competing model while still on our \$0.03 legacy deal? (Internal) Ways to make the Case Study even more challenging: 1. **Introduce a tension between two stakeholders.** "BFL's Head of Accounting believes resellers are critical because they reduce infrastructure burden and allow the team to focus on model development. The head of GTM wants to maximize direct revenue. Your strategy needs to address both perspectives." This tests whether they can navigate internal politics, not just external partnerships. 2. **Add a live curveball during Q&A.** Instead of just asking follow-up questions, we hand them a "breaking news" update mid-presentation (e.g., "Replicate just announced a 40% price cut on all image models and is promoting Nano Banana as their featured model.") Give them 5 minutes to adapt their recommendation on the spot. 3. **Include a role-play negotiation as a second component.** After the presentation, have one interviewer play a reseller partner (say, Runware’s CEO) who's pushing to renegotiate terms down to 15% rev-share while threatening to deprioritize FLUX in favor of Nano Banana. Give the candidate 15 minutes to negotiate. This would replace part of the Q&A time. ### Archive/Sctratchpad {toggle="true"} **Interviewer 1 ** **Strategic thinking, fast-learner, understand complex orgs/concepts, ability to work in ambiguity** Interviewer 1 checks on strategic / bigger picture experience of candidate - Tell me about the most complex deal you’ve worked on, and what made it complicated? - What were the strategic trade-offs that you had to consider as part of the deal? - Were there internal stakeholders who were hesitant about it? Why? What did you do to change their mind? - how did you do initial research on the business strategy of the customer/partner? - Give me an example of a deal where you had a learn about a new business model and/or technical concept. How did you go about this? - What would you consider the biggest challenges that Black Forest Labs might be facing in our effort to build high value and sustainable partnerships? - How do you build champions inside an account, especially in complex environments? - Tell me about a time when you deliberately lost a deal or walked away. Why, and what was your strategy? - What is the least favorite part of your job **Interviewer 2** **Territory / pipeline management**: Explain your last territory / account set (depending on past experience), the strategy you have created for it, how you have executed it and results. - S: - Explain more details around # of accounts, regions, verticals, company type and size (ENT, SUP, SMB, etc.), new territory, same as last year, etc. - Existing pipeline already? If yes, how did you prioritize it? - GFD, EGD, mix? - What prio for company you worked for? - Focus accounts, long-tail, etc.? - What were you selling? SaaS, license, AI-models, compute, etc.? - Were you alone? How did your account team look like? - T: - What was your quota? What the baseline revenue you were coming from? - Did you have other KPIs, e.g. upselling, closing large commitments, etc.? - Were there specific “must-win accounts” or sth. like that? - How were the goals set? - A: - How did you segment and prioritize your accounts? - How did you structure and prioritize your pipeline? Do you track specific metrics? - How do you make sure that nothing falls through the cracks? - How do you forecast? Bottoms-up / top-down? - With whom are you working together and for what deals? - In case you have a long-tail, how do you approach it? - Did you create a playbook for yourself / your team? - R: - How did you track results / what goal cadence did you have (month, quarterly, yearly, etc.) - How did you perform against your set of goals? - What were key drivers? Was it simply riding the wave or can you tell me about specific initiatives you were driving that resulted in this success? - R: - In hindsight what would you do differently? - What are key learning that you would apply to BFL? **Lighthouse deal: **It’s super important for startups like to BFL to win lighthouse customers. Tell me about a deal that you are really proud of, where you went the extra mile, won a lighthouse deal and what you’ve made out of it. - S - Tell me more about the account - How long did you work with the account? - Was it pure GFD? Or already somehow with a relationship / revenue? - Who was on the account team? **Scale operations / sales process: **Startups need to do things that scale. Tell me about a situation where you have scaled sales significantly. (In case candidate is not sure what’s meant: Think about a situation where you saw that things were repetitive, involved significant overhead / manual labor, simply saw potential to make a process faster, self-serve, etc.) **Andi: knowledge of space, technical understanding, anything else the first interviewers flagged** - to check on technical understanding (sufficient for sales) and overall BFL / culture fit, could potentially run a mock customer conversation as a technical interested buyer, e.g. PM role, startup founder role? - general motivations + knowledge of the competitive landscape: why are you excited about joining BFL vs other genAI companies? - what are your favorite tools in the image generation space and why? - From your perception of BFL, how would you describe our business model? - knowledge of the open source space: - what do you think makes BFL special and different from other media generation companies or big tech firms that offer image/video generation solutions? - OS - From your experience, what might be general challenges regarding the business model and legal risks for a OS model provider like BFL? - business model: how to monetize OS - legal: copyright (stability case), illegal content for open models (how to control) - Resolving critical points in negotiations + knowledge about risks when being a model provider: - indemnification —\> counterparty asking for full indemnitiy including 3p rights; us only giving patent rights. - what are the challenges and risks for us especially around 3p rights? - How can we resolve? - On-site: could be mock sales conversation, working on a sales deal, how to solve the dev license scenario, etc. - Potentially Robin interview if needed STARR Question Bank "}

To help us better coordinate office visits and ensure we're prepared when team members, clients, candidates, or other external visitors come to the SF Office:
## What to Do
When you or anyone else will be visiting our office, please add the visit to our [BFL Calendar](https://calendar.google.com/calendar/embed?src=c_77cf5b596fb7704516f85dafcb58fc31084e9000cf3629d8cc93b96c77baed33%40group.calendar.google.com&ctz=Europe%2FBerlin) with the following information:
- **Dates of the visit** - Include all days you’ll be in town
- **Who is visiting** - Name(s) of visitors with emails, so we may add them to Forkable if they are staying for lunch
- **Number of people** - If applicable (e.g., "Client + 2 team members")
- **Put Melissa in CC on the calendar invite** - This helps maintain visibility and coordinate as needed
## When to Add
Please add visits to the calendar as soon as they're confirmed, even if details are still being finalized. You can always update the calendar event later if plans change.
## Why This Helps
Having this information on our shared calendar allows us to:
- Plan ahead for office space and resources
- Coordinate schedules when multiple visitors are in town
- Prepare for enough food for everyone joining
- Ensure a smooth experience for our guests
</content>

title: Speaker Guardrails & Prep Guide
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Speaker Guardrails & Prep Guide","url":"https://www.notion.so/31fc370222d581afad05ded11d24be2e","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/31fc370222d581afad05ded11d24be2e as of 2026-03-10T13:59:37.912Z: {"title":"Speaker Guardrails & Prep Guide"} Reference this before any external appearance — podcast, conference, panel, or interview. These guardrails apply to **everyone** representing BFL, not just founders. --- ## Who We Are (and Are Not) When speaking externally, always anchor on our identity: **We are:** The frontier AI research lab powering visual intelligence everywhere. We ship world-class research at commercial speed. We're the default for frontier developers and pro creatives — best models, open weights, multi-cloud, no lock-in. **We are not:** - "The open-source Midjourney" (consumer framing) - "The cheaper Google alternative" (race to bottom) - "An image generation tool" (we're a research lab building visual intelligence infrastructure) - "The EU sovereign alternative" (no strategic advantage without global framing) --- ## Spokesperson Beats Each speaker should stay in their lane. If a question falls outside your beat, it's fine to say "that's more \[name\]'s area" and redirect.
Beat Core Topics Who Typically Covers
**Vision & Research** Future of visual AI, research philosophy, long-term direction, "why we exist" Robin, Axel
**Product & Commercial** Enterprise use cases, product launches, "why companies choose us," partnerships Andi
**Policy & Safety** EU AI Act, responsible AI, governance, trust Ben, Adam
**Developer Education** How to build with FLUX, tutorials, open source, developer workflows DevRel team
**Operations & Culture** Scaling from Europe, hiring, team culture, research DNA COO / People
**Partnerships** Integrations, co-marketing, ecosystem BD/Partnerships
--- ## Before You Go Out: Prep Checklist - [ ] **Check the tracker** — log your appearance in the Speaking & Appearances Tracker - [ ] **Know your beat** — stay in your lane, redirect what's outside it - [ ] **Review key messages** — read the current BFL narrative doc and latest product positioning - [ ] **Flag sensitive topics** — if the host wants to discuss competitors, pricing, unreleased products, or safety controversies, flag to Comms before the appearance - [ ] **Request a briefing** — check "Help Needed" in the tracker if you want talking points, a briefing packet, or a dry run - [ ] **Confirm with Comms** — any Tier 1 media (Bloomberg, Economist, Fortune, etc.) or high-stakes appearances need Comms sign-off --- ## Topics That Require Comms Approval Do not freelance on these — loop in Comms/PR before discussing: - Unreleased products or timelines (FLUX.3, new modalities) - Fundraising, valuation, M&A - Competitor comparisons (especially Google, Midjourney, Stability) - Regulatory positions or policy stances - Internal company metrics (revenue, headcount specifics, customer names without approval) - Anything related to safety incidents or controversies --- ## Talking Points Style Guide **Do:** - Lead with what we enable, not just what we built - Use concrete examples and customer stories (approved ones) - Emphasize the research-to-production pipeline — we don't just publish papers, we ship - Highlight open weights and developer empowerment - Be authentic — people connect with the person, not the pitch **Don't:** - Trash competitors directly — frame as "our approach is different because..." - Promise specific timelines for unreleased features - Speculate on industry consolidation or others' business models - Use overly technical jargon for non-technical audiences - Claim "we're the best" without specifics — instead, point to benchmarks, downloads (400M+), or customer outcomes --- ## After the Appearance - [ ] Update the tracker with the recording link and actual reach if available - [ ] Flag anything noteworthy to Comms (unexpected questions, competitor mentions, follow-up requests) - [ ] Share the recording or link on Slack so the team can amplify --- ## Need Help? Check the **"Help Needed"** box in the Speaking & Appearances Tracker and describe what you need in **Support Notes**. Comms/Marketing will pick it up. For urgent prep (\< 48 hours), ping the marketing channel directly. "}

title: Strategic finance/FP&A
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Strategic finance/FP&A","url":"https://www.notion.so/2f0c370222d580739b20f5f9d6646d0a","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2f0c370222d580739b20f5f9d6646d0a as of 2026-03-31T15:37:00.872Z: {"title":"Strategic finance/FP&A"} ## The Role We're looking for a strategic finance leader who can bring structure to high-growth chaos. As our first dedicated FP&A, you'll be the financial architect behind our scaling decisions—translating our rapid growth into clear financial frameworks, building robust planning processes, and partnering with leadership to make disciplined decisions about where and how to invest. This is a high-impact, hands-on role. You'll own the company's financial planning muscle, work directly with finance leadership and executive team, and have visibility into every major business decision. You'll be comfortable operating across our US and German entities, understanding the complexities of international operations, and building scalable processes that work across borders. If you're energized by turning ambiguity into clarity, love building systems from scratch, and want direct impact on a fast-scaling AI company, we'd love to meet you. ## What You'll Do ### Core Responsibilities **Financial Planning & Forecasting** - Own and drive the full planning cycle: annual operating plans, quarterly forecasts, rolling projections, and long-range strategic planning - Build and maintain sophisticated financial models covering revenue (API, Playground, Enterprise), expenses, headcount, GPU compute costs and model building complexity as well as cash flow across the group. - Lead scenario planning and sensitivity analysis for major decisions (GPU provider contracts, go-to-market expansion, pricing frameworks) - Drive continuous improvement in forecast accuracy as the business scales **Business Partnership** - Partner with GTM leadership on revenue forecasting, customer segmentation economics, pricing strategy, and capacity planning - Collaborate with Engineering on GPU compute optimization, infrastructure planning, and R&D investment allocation - Support Product on feature prioritization, monetization analysis, and competitive positioning - Translate strategy into financial reality—surfacing tradeoffs, forcing clarity, and ensuring alignment between ambition and resources **Performance Management & Insights** - Deliver monthly and quarterly business reviews with variance analysis, KPIs, and actionable insights - Build executive dashboards that track key metrics: ARR growth, customer cohort economics, gross margins, burn rate, runway - Analyze the P&L across our multiple revenue streams and identify opportunities for margin expansion and efficiency - Help craft compelling financial narratives for board meetings, investor updates, and strategic planning sessions **Systems & Process Excellence** - Design and implement scalable FP&A processes that work with a growing, fast moving company in a new space - Partner with Accounting to ensure close process efficiency, data integrity, and reporting consistency - Drive automation and AI enablement across financial planning and reporting - Build the infrastructure (tools, templates, workflows) needed to support 3-5x growth **Strategic Initiatives** - Support high-impact projects: pricing optimization, enterprise contract structuring, M&A evaluation, fundraising support - Work with Rev Ops in building customer segmentation frameworks and analyze unit economics by customer type, geography, and product ## What Success Looks Like ### First 30 Days - Learn & Assess - Understand our business model deeply: revenue streams, customer base, pricing mechanics, cost structure - Audit existing financial models, forecasts, and reporting processes—identify gaps and quick wins - Build relationships with key stakeholders: Chief of Staff, Engineering leads and founders - Gain fluency in our GPU compute economics and infrastructure costs - Deliver initial observations and recommendations on planning process improvements ### First 60 Days - Build & Improve - Own the next quarterly forecast cycle end-to-end with improved accuracy and granularity - Establish monthly business review cadence with consistent KPIs, variance analysis, and executive reporting - Create or significantly enhance core financial models: revenue by stream, customer cohort analysis, headcount planning, cash flow forecasting - Implement 2-3 quick process improvements that increase efficiency or data quality - Partner with GTM on refined revenue forecasting methodology incorporating pipeline visibility - Begin designing the framework for annual planning cycle ### First 90 Days - Lead & Scale - Lead any reforecasting process with bottoms-up input from all departments - Help craft board-ready materials demonstrating financial performance, trends, and strategic recommendations - Establish yourself as the trusted financial advisor to executive team and department leaders - Deliver tangible business impact: better decisions, clearer tradeoffs, improved forecast accuracy, or process efficiency gains - Identify and begin implementing 1-2 strategic initiatives (pricing optimization, customer segmentation economics, scenario planning framework) ## What You Bring ### Essential Requirements **Experience** - 6-10 years in FP&A, corporate finance, investment banking, consulting, or strategic finance - Minimum 4 years hands-on FP&A experience at a high-growth company - Proven track record owning full planning cycles (annual budgeting, quarterly forecasts, long-range planning) - Experience with B2B AI or SaaS or technology businesses; understanding of subscription economics, usage-based pricing, and enterprise sales - Comfort with international operations or multi-entity financial structures **Technical Skills** - Advanced Excel/Google Sheets with strong financial modeling capabilities—you can build complex models from scratch - Experience with modern finance tech stack and curiosity around AI improvements and possibilities against legacy tech stack incumbents - Understanding of SaaS metrics: ARR/MRR, NDR, CAC, LTV, payback period, gross margin, Rule of 40 and ideally experience with consumption based metrics - Ability to work with large datasets, perform variance analysis, and build dashboards - Financial statement literacy and understanding of US GAAP **Interview Process** Screening First interview: Dave Arkell Second interview: Sarah/ Adam- Aim to asses cultural fit/values alignment things to test for: Suggest Sarah test agency/speed and Adam test culture and prioritisation - **High agency/ownership** - *Tell me about a time you identified a problem at work that wasn't in your job description and fixed it anyway. What happened?* - *Give me an example of a decision you made with limited information that turned out to be right — and one that turned out to be wrong. What did you do differently after the second one?* - *When did you last disagree with your manager about how to approach something? What did you do?* - *Tell me about a project you owned end to end. What would have happened if you hadn't pushed it forward?* - *Have you ever taken on a responsibility that was clearly above your pay grade/scope? What drove you to do it?* - **Operating with ambiguity and speed** - *How do you personally decide when you have enough information to act versus when to keep gathering data?* - *Tell me about a time a key assumption in your plan turned out to be wrong mid-execution. What did you do?* - *Tell me about a time you had to present a forecast you weren't fully confident in. How did you frame it, and what happened?* - *Have you ever been pressured to move faster on a model or report than you were comfortable with? How did you handle it?* - *When do you think it's acceptable to present numbers you know are directionally right but not fully reconciled? Where do you draw the line?* - *Give me an example of a financial analysis you did that turned out to be more precise than the situation actually needed. What would you do differently?* - *How do you decide what level of detail is enough in a model — and how has that judgment changed over your career?* - **Prioritisation under pressure** - *Walk me through a month-end close or forecast cycle where everything went wrong at the same time. What did you triage and why?* - *Tell me about a time a senior stakeholder asked for a completely new analysis mid-cycle. How did you balance that with existing commitments?* - *What's the thing you most consistently have to let go of — in terms of quality or completeness — when time is short? Does that bother you?* - **BFL specific cultural fit** - *What do you find genuinely interesting about what BFL is building? What aspect of the product or technology have you spent time trying to understand?* - *Have you ever had to get your head around a completely new technical domain quickly — compute infrastructure, a new business model, a new regulatory regime? How did you go about it?* - *Tell me about a time you worked closely with engineers or researchers who thought very differently from you. What did you learn, and what friction did you encounter?* - *What does "good" look like to you in a fast-scaling company — and how is that different from a large, established one?* - *When have you had to push back on something senior leadership wanted to do? How did you frame it?* Third interview: Robin - looking at how well he could work with them Case study on-site

**Case Study** 1. Revenue forecasting 1. Give historic MRR reporting (and caveat that there are billing errors) 2. Show historical trends with both our and other model releases 3. Give roadmap of next model releases 4. Show sales headcount evolution 5. Ask to produce a revenue forecast for the next 6 months based on those inputs 1. Cost planning 1. Attached are our historic costs, current headcount evolution and some of our broader strategies/bets that we may be considering. Put together a template for us to be able to model costs and how we can quickly assess some of the cost options. Things to include as part of case study 1. Include inference being RI 2. include historical GPU purchases plus tracking of storage 3. Show some historical data acquisition costs 4. Show historical headcount with some degree of roster 5. Brief comments on rent and other overheads as well as travel philosophy 6. Legal being high given complexity and risks of an AI business Case study - master **Tiffany Kha- **Case study Case study - Markus Tiffany Kha (AC Feedback) "}

</properties>
<content>
For remote whiteboarding 
- [https://excalidraw.com/](https://excalidraw.com/)
**Timing** 
- 1 hour 
**Structure**:
- Introductions - 2-3 min
- Brief discussion of technical assignment - we ask any questions we had (if the assignment  raised any questions) - timing depends on a situation but good to keep it minimal. Sometimes it can take longer if assignment raised questions we wanna clear up.  
- We move onto the system design discussion - 45 min
- We reserve time for the end section - questions listed below.  7-8 min
# Task Overview
Context: 
You have just implemented a small computation takes **\~5 seconds** per task. The worker loads a large model on startup (\~40 seconds cold start). 
# Communication with Candidate 
# Rubric
1. Where would you place broker, task backend, postgres etc and how would communication go end to end for one task ?  How would you provide the task result to the customer who submitted the task ? 
2. Your company has acquired a second GPU cluster in the same region. It has identical hardware.
	-  How do you distribute tasks across the two clusters? What are the tradeoffs between a shared queue vs. per-cluster queues with a router?
	-  At worker startup it loads a large model into GPU memory. How does this affect your scaling strategy compared to stateless workers? What happens when you need to roll out a model update across both clusters?
	- What happens if one cluster goes offline? How does the system detect this and react? Consider what happens to in-flight tasks on the failed cluster.
	- How do you ensure result retrieval still works when the task may have been processed by either cluster?
3. You are expanding from **US-East** to **EU-West** to reduce latency for European users and comply with data residency requirements. 
	- Draw or describe the target architecture. Which components are regional and which are global?
	- Users and their credit balances: does each region get its own database, or do they share one? What are the consistency implications of each choice?
	- \[Depend on the previous answer\]A user submits a task in EU-West but their account was created in US-East. How does authentication and credit deduction work?
	- Task routing: should a task submitted in EU-West always be processed by EU-West GPU workers, or can it overflow to US-East? What are the latency and cost implications?
	- How do you handle a regional outage? Can EU users fail over to US, and what does that mean for data residency?
4. Add a priority system - Product wants to offer **three tiers**: Free, Pro, and Enterprise. Enterprise tasks should be processed before Pro, and Pro before Free — but no tier should be fully starved.
	- How do you implement priority at the queue level? Consider weighted fair queuing, separate queues with priority consumers, or other approaches.
	- What happens to priority ordering when you have multiple clusters and regions from Parts 1 and 2?
	- An Enterprise user submits 10,000 tasks at once. How do you prevent this from starving other Enterprise users? Is per-user fairness different from per-tier priority?
5. Scale this architecture 100x - 
Traffic has grown 100x from the original design. You now serve 50,000 concurrent users submitting \~200 tasks/second across both regions.
Discuss the evolution of bottlenecks as you scale up. For each bottleneck, explain how you would address it and what becomes the next bottleneck after that.
1. Cascading failures - scalability event aka new model launch with unpredictable traffic.
You are launching a new model. Based on previous launches, you expect a **10–50x traffic spike** within the first hour, but the exact magnitude is unknown. The spike is bursty — it may come in waves as social media posts go viral.
<empty-block/>
**Guidelines for discussion: **
- There are no single correct answers. We are looking for structured thinking, awareness of tradeoffs, and the ability to reason about failure modes.
- Feel free to draw diagrams, write pseudocode, or reference specific technologies.
- When you propose a solution, also state what it does NOT solve or what new problem it introduces.
- If you make an assumption, state it explicitly. 
<empty-block/>
**At the end:**
- Ask the candidate feedback on technical assignment
- Ask the candidate if they feel they had a fair chance to represent themselves in this round 
- Reserve time for candidate’s questions to us
<empty-block/>
</content>
</page>"}

title: Technical Project Discussion — Interview Guide (Infrastructure)
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Technical Project Discussion — Interview Guide (Infrastructure)","url":"https://www.notion.so/32fc370222d580508235e658c1acd49f","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/32fc370222d580508235e658c1acd49f as of 2026-04-02T22:11:55.700Z: {"title":"Technical Project Discussion — Interview Guide (Infrastructure)"} Evaluate the candidate’s technical ownership, decision-making, and ability to deeply understand and reflect on complex systems they’ve built. This is a deep dive into ONE past project. Focus on: - ownership and contributions - system design and architecture - technical decision-making and tradeoffs - debugging and problem-solving - ability to reflect and improve systems ## What Good Looks Like Strong candidates will: - clearly explain a complex system end-to-end - demonstrate real ownership (not just participation) - explain why decisions were made (not just what) - discuss tradeoffs and alternatives - walk through real failures or challenges - reflect on what they would do differently ## Core Question Here's how we'll structure it: you'll have about 15 minutes to walk me through the project uninterrupted - the architecture, the key decisions you made, the trade-offs, and the challenges. I won't cut in during that time. After that, I'll go deep with questions for about 20 minutes. Then we'll end with a retro - how you'd approach it differently today. We'll save the last 5 minutes for your questions. Any questions before we start?"

"Go ahead - take a moment to think about which project you want to walk me through. It should be something where you made meaningful technical decisions and faced real constraints. Ready when you are." "Hi \[name\], welcome. I'm \[your name\] - I'm on \[team\], focused on \[responsibilities\]. Today's format is a bit different from a typical interview. I want to hear you go really deep on one project - the most technically complex thing you've worked on, ideally in the ML infrastructure space. No slides needed; I care about the substance, not the presentation.
Candidate Presentation (15 min) > Do not interrupt during this phase. Your job is to listen and take notes. If they go off on a tangent, let them - it often reveals what they actually care about. If they finish early (under 8 min), that's a signal in itself.
What to listen for? - Depth markers - note when you hear these - Do they lead with "what" or "why"? Strong candidates explain reasoning before mechanics. - Do they name specific systems, numbers, constraints - or stay at abstract level? - Do they acknowledge trade-offs unprompted, or present everything as the obvious right call? - Do they mention other teams, stakeholders, pushback? Or present as if they worked in a vacuum? - How do they talk about failure? Do they surface it voluntarily, minimize it, or skip it entirely? - Note-taking prompts (jot for Q&A) - Any decision they made that sounds under-explained - you'll push on this - Any number that sounds impressive - verify it. - Any team dynamic they glossed over - ask about it - Any technology choice that wasn't justified — surface it
Deep Q&A ( \~ 20 min) ”Thanks - really interesting. I'm going to go deep now. Some of my questions will be about things you mentioned, some will push into areas you didn't cover. There are no trick questions - I just want to understand how you think.”
Q1: Architecture and design decisions - “You chose \[X\]. Walk me through why that over \[Y\]”
Frame it as - "You mentioned \[decision\]. What were the real alternatives you considered, and what ruled them out?" - "At the time, what were you most uncertain about in that choice?" - "If someone on your team pushed back on that approach, what would their strongest argument have been?"
Listen for - Can they steelman the alternative? Weak candidates can only defend their choice, not articulate the opponent's case. - Is their reasoning based on data/constraints, or post-hoc rationalization? - Positives: - Names concrete constraints that drove the choice - Acknowledges what they gave up - Negatives: - Every choice was "obvious" or "best practice"
Q2: Scale and constraints - “What broke first as this scaled, and how did you know it was going to break before it did?”
Variations - "What were the hard limits of your design - the ceiling you knew you'd eventually hit?" - "What assumptions in your architecture would have needed to change at 10x the load?" - "How did you validate it would hold at scale before you committed to it?"
Listen for - Do they have mental models for failure modes, or did they discover problems reactively? - Can they distinguish what they knew vs. what they discovered?
Positives - Anticipates bottlenecks before they happened - Has numbers - not just "it scaled well"
- Negatives - Can only describe what broke, not why it was going to
Q3: Hardest technical problem - “What was the single hardest problem you hit, and walk me through how you actually solved it step by step”
Push on process, not just outcome - "Walk me through your debugging process - what did you try first, what eliminated what?" - "What was your hypothesis going in, and when did it turn out to be wrong?" - "How long did it take, and what eventually cracked it?"
Listen for - Do they have a systematic method, or did they stumble into the answer? - Can they reconstruct their mental state at the time - not just the clean retrospective version?
Positives: - Describes what they ruled out and why - Admits they were wrong initially
Negatives - Solution arrived via luck or someone else - worth noting - Jumps straight to answer with no process
Q4: Team & cross-functional dynamics - “How many teams were involved, and where did you hit the most friction?”
Variations - "Who pushed back hardest on your approach, and what was their concern?" - "How did you get alignment when teams had different priorities or timelines?" - "Was there a decision you made that someone else owned - how did you navigate that?"
Listen for - Do they talk about people and dynamics specifically, or abstractly? ("we aligned" vs. how they actually aligned) - Do they acknowledge that others had valid concerns, or were all dissenters just wrong?
Positives - Names the person/team and their actual concern - Describes influence without authority
Negatives - Everyone agreed, no pushback - suspicious - Dismissive of other teams' concerns
Q5: Ownership depth - “Which parts of this did you personally design vs inherit or implement someone else’s spec?”
Push if needed - "On \[specific component\] - were you the one who decided on that approach, or were you executing on a direction that was already set?" - "If this project had gone sideways, which parts would have been on you?"
Listen for - Honest ownership vs. claiming credit for the team's work. This usually reveals itself in specificity - real owners have opinions on the details.
Positives - Can say "I didn't decide X, that was \[person\]" - Has strong opinions on their own scope
Negatives - Fuzzy on what they personally contributed
Retro: What they’d do differently with today’s knowledge (12 min) "Let's shift into retro mode. Forget what was possible at the time - if you were starting this project today, with everything you now know, how would you do it differently? I'm interested in both the technical choices and how you'd run the project.”
R1: Technical retro: “What’s the one architectural decision you’d reverse, and what would you replace it with?”
Push past surface-level answers - "Is that something you would have known at the time if you'd had more information, or did it require the experience of running it?" - "What did you learn from that mistake that you've applied since?"
Watch out for - "I'd document better" or "I'd write more tests" - these are safe answers that signal low self-awareness. Push: "Okay, but technically - what would you actually change about the design?" - Strong answers name a specific design choice, explain why it was wrong, and describe concretely what they'd replace it with - including the new trade-offs that introduces.
R2: Process retro: “How would you run the project differently - team structure, decision making, how you handled uncertainty?”
Variations - "Were there decisions that took too long to make? What slowed them down?" - "Looking back, what did you learn too late - what signal did you have early but didn't act on?" - "Was there a moment where the team's morale or alignment broke down? What would you do differently there?"
Listen for - Genuine retrospection vs. corporate retrospection ("we could have communicated better"). - Strong candidates name specific moments and specific people.
R3: Growth signal: “What did this project teach you that you couldn’t have learned any other way?”
Listen for: - Intellectual honesty - do they credit the project for real learning, or just recount accomplishments?\\ - Transfer - have they actually applied what they learned, or just identified it?
Positives: - Names a belief they held that turned out to be wrong - Points to how it changed their next project
Negatives: - Lessons are generic ("importance of communication")
## Areas to Explore ### Project Context - What problem was the system solving? - What was the scale and scope? - What was your specific role? ### System Architecture - How was the system designed? - What were the key components? - What were the most important design decisions? - What tradeoffs did you consider? ### Challenges & Debugging - What were the hardest technical problems? - What broke at scale? - How did you diagnose and fix issues? - Any major incidents or failures? ### Impact - What impact did the system have? - How was success measured? - What changed because of this work? ### Retrospective - What worked well? - What didn’t work well? - What would you do differently today? ## What to Probe - What specifically did YOU own vs the team? - Why did you choose that approach over alternatives? - What was the first bottleneck you hit? - How did the system behave at scale? - What would break at 10x scale? - What tradeoffs did you knowingly accept? ## Evaluation Criteria Strong Yes: - Clear ownership of a complex system - Deep understanding of architecture and tradeoffs - Strong debugging and problem-solving examples - Thoughtful reflection and learning Yes: - Solid project experience with some ownership - Good understanding, but less depth or scale - Can explain decisions with some prompting No: - Vague or surface-level explanations - Cannot clearly explain their role or contributions - Lacks understanding of tradeoffs or system behavior - No meaningful debugging or failure experience "}

<callout icon="🎄" color="gray_bg">
	Next company wide closure during Christmas: 24 Dec. 2025 - 2 Jan. 2026. Please submit these days in Rippling as PTO.
</callout>
# Time off Philosophy
Our time off policy is flexible time off, in the sense that you can take what you need. Like work, we approach our time off with high ownership, and want to acknowledge that everyone is working hard to make BFL successful. 
We offer flexible paid time off, with the expectation that everyone takes **at least **the statutory allowance shown in your Rippling profile. 
<empty-block/>
**Note **
- This policy applies globally. 
- In Rippling, under **My Time**, you see your total holiday balance, which aligns with local statutory requirements. Make sure to use it all and have your balance at **0 or negative by the end of the year. **You can go into negative balance without any impact, all submitted time off days are paid. 
- All balances reset at the start of the year, no days accrue. 
- All leave is tracked through Rippling. Submit all your leave days include PTO, Sick Day, Child Sick day, Special leave, etc. through Rippling. 
- Please also log any public holidays you take in Rippling, so our teams across different countries stay aligned. These will **not **be deducted from your total holiday balance.
<callout icon="☝" color="gray_bg">
	For people hired through [Remote.com](http://Remote.com) - Please log in all your leave days on the Remote portal. 
</callout>
# **Standard Operating Procedure **
When you take time off, do the following: 
**Plan**
- Notify your team at minimum 2x the length of planned leave in advance
- For 2+consecutive weeks outside of the Christmas period, please ask your team lead 
- Submit requests through Rippling, once you have used your statutory days, your balance will go into negative 
- Ensure no conflicts with team deliverables like new releases or key meetings like offsites 
**Prepare**
- **Block your calendar using "Out of Office" instead of Event in your calendar. This automatically updates Slack so people are aware you’re away.**
- Ensure nothing will be blocked on you during this time. Either close out or delegate ongoing items and ensure there is an escalation path. Create a handover document for any ongoing projects if needed. 
- Enable email auto-response if you won’t check your email 
# Global vacation, public holiday & birthday calendar 
Get visibility into when someone might be off. 
Click on "+" next to "other calendars" and add URL.
