title: Unstructured Thoughts from Cross-Functional Day
content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Unstructured Thoughts from Cross-Functional Day","url":"https://www.notion.so/342c370222d580c783fce18e6b069c7a","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/342c370222d580c783fce18e6b069c7a as of 2026-04-15T13:20:21.016Z: {"title":"Unstructured Thoughts from Cross-Functional Day"} - How do we tweak the standard OKR/rev-focused operating playbooks to help accelerate BFL’s research first focus? - Need to make presentations/discussions more data-driven and factual: e.g. what is actual TAM per use case? e.g. Andi’s example on fal for GTM, e.g. Anthony’s analysis on Q1 update - There’s still a lot of open questions and uncertainty about direction of the business. We need a consistent mechanism to (a) collect these (b) assign owners to answer them (c) feedback to the group for visibility/accountability - In other words, how do we avoid being paralysed by unknowns and break it down into simpler action items to make faster decisions - Sessions felt quite high level + switching context too much: we need to get crisper with being clear on each session’s outcome beforehand. Do we want to make practical decisions? Do we want to give visibility to the group? Do we want to agree on priorities? - Might make sense to start with a strong view and then debate that vs. starting bottoms up to speed up the process - We need to rethink forums for the sessions: for example for headcount there were moments were not everyone was needed. Could we have done this more efficiently? On the other hand we’re missing key people for some decisions (e.g. Sandeep in infra) and it was good to have Justine involved in headcount session to accelerate decisions and cut middle layer \> IC information relay - As per Morgan’s feedback: how do we think about the longer term mission for the company and not just on Flux3 release/short-term goals? "}

title: VAE/SSL Pre-training
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"VAE/SSL Pre-training","url":"https://www.notion.so/317c370222d5805fbac6fb1734902f80","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/317c370222d5805fbac6fb1734902f80 as of 2026-04-18T13:37:09.456Z: {"title":"VAE/SSL Pre-training"} # VAE+SSL Joint Pre-training for Video ## Research Question / Hypothesis Can we make video VAE latents more learnable by jointly training with SSL objectives (DINO, [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471)) — while keeping reconstruction quality intact? And if the learned representations are strong enough, can the encoder double as a foundation for downstream conditioning and planning? The core idea: reconstruction-only VAE training produces latents biased toward low-level pixel info. More training compute → better reconstruction but generation quality stagnates or gets worse. [VTP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) showed this clearly for images (see Fig 1 below). Adding understanding objectives (CLIP, SSL) fixes this — generation improves with compute. We want to do this for video, where temporal semantics matter and image-based SSL (like what [REPA-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) uses) isn't enough. **Hypotheses:** - Joint VAE+SSL training injects semantic structure into latents → better learnability for downstream diffusion - V-JEPA style objectives may be better than DINO for video since they capture motion/temporal stuff. V-JEPA 2 hits 77.3% on SSv2 with a frozen encoder + attentive probe — that's pure motion understanding from SSL alone, no labels during pre-training. More importantly, it shows these representations transfer to planning: the same encoder enables zero-shot robot control after minimal post-training. This is the kind of latent structure we want in our VAE — if SSL quality is high enough, the encoder becomes reusable for downstream conditioning and planning, not just tokenization. - This should scale — more VAE pre-training compute should keep helping generation (unlike rec-only which plateaus) ### Core figure from [VTP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) (Yao et al., 2025) ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/49acc9e0-3573-480b-8010-4e8081940b67/Screenshot_2026-03-02_at_9.54.07_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466V5C6XCYA%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T152300Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIBhaRZiLC7JWqcE%2Bb8TNWmYu08lIA4%2Bf4j6y7tOiXkfqAiEA522UGoQLzRTlyn2kP0JA3IM9oXJbKngJtRYqABid1eIq%2FwMICBAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDJi7gm6HOJ7GUvjhZSrcA41XbNYCIk1Cp9EDShJhFfrck1oKW5eAyoFAuWxJQ20tbcgCo%2BbvNPwdQywVkFN5%2BYdc4T%2Fqff4aP5m6VoAmCFphcBuQ5nT2NmlATGOlVU85JRkPVnUgMxnqtcruw3iUhidznzUx7lrjkVPQ%2BdiGONWmXDW%2BarhI1%2BZgHYhMruslxYrvXHaddwe%2B7trdOxYWRodldqSEQ%2Fq%2FS5Eq2CA2C8SGBjiyhEsg0gFWk8z3XJOxj%2FHzpIIJIBHRg%2FEu6niSSz%2Bsk8HFpeRlbNzkWgtvpz20gEcb%2BTNABPggxQHUIx78voW0UuXKZCtpbNffU4qJ8RXG%2BCvahLELrZKPDqsEh2frzowvWwC9PporknWksrwDnkn%2BLHBW7PiizL0N0sQhDd5KDXhXud5dnCwElQK1lsgy1wbLNUFe8bpCq%2FVKZb33W61tXfqkR3ZUqU4JjCO5s%2B6nTQatIfizLe4%2B1j6WgvIXiLoPusBltWhhUUiD2hMY1BfsH2WAydUftj2g%2Fp3y%2FwFEFVlz9UkVZVk8rhRoK9RiQJJv28%2BlHVzTQJXmY4GFk2hAtSbrsTgwmXv7aWktVq19b93FKJ91yqKnp%2FA202tJGma6mZlZ%2BfqnEypTmWYMEE8gRMW28dTniUY2MMDQk88GOqUBXOrN03AeSpKU0t3GdCZtxkP%2B8Fa6SHrENIKEDDZIJbLxnP2E2u2X3ubWUkzE8gBqCQhMEgQ90F1yM9BMLQU%2BcRfNoOZxEjzvxKwN3b5RP7fube52BhCNlJWiubsFSIU4qOQLPB%2FXVgsk5qbKpket916JGuIdPq0EqyEw%2F8IoB4V0cGgkP5NnhTjT4KcrmYylCIm6wZymKB49pYE9d86PLPJhRivk&X-Amz-Signature=79fe210706f95736614a9a7112d81632966dccb57eb1537ca2d29ce6daa78981&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) *Fig 1: From VTP paper. SSL+AE and CLIP+AE show correlated growth in generation and understanding with compute. Reconstruction-only AE stagnates. We want to replicate this behavior for video with video-native SSL.* ## Why this matters Current approaches each have clear problems (see also [BFL's representation comparison](https://bfl.ai/research/representation-comparison) and [Sander Dieleman's latent space post](https://sander.ai/2025/04/15/latents.html) for broader context on the learnability-reconstruction trade-off): - [**RAE**](https://rae-dit.github.io/) (frozen DINOv2 + trained decoder): Good learnability but reconstruction is bad — color shifts, texture errors. Frozen image encoder, no temporal understanding for video. - [**REPA-E**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) (end-to-end VAE+diffusion via REPA loss): Strong image results but ties VAE optimization to diffusion training. Uses DINOv2 which is image-only — not ideal for video. - [**VTP**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) (CLIP+SSL+rec for images): Proves the scaling thesis but image-only, hasn't been extended to video. Our angle: **video-native SSL directly in VAE pre-training, decoupled from diffusion**. This gives us: - Reusable tokenizer (not entangled with diffusion like REPA-E) - Trainable encoder with reconstruction loss (not frozen like RAE) - Temporal understanding from [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471) / [V-JEPA 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) - Potential encoder reuse for conditioning and planning — if probe accuracy is high enough, the encoder has generic video understanding and can serve as a conditioning backbone. V-JEPA 2 demonstrates this concretely: their self-supervised video encoder, after post-training with just 62 hours of unlabeled robot data, enables zero-shot robotic planning via model predictive control in latent space — picking and placing objects in unseen environments without any task-specific training or reward. If our VAE encoder internalizes similar temporal-semantic structure through the JEPA objective, it could serve not just as a tokenizer but as the backbone of a world model for planning and action-conditioned generation. The learned latent space could also be used to train a separate V-JEPA-style planning model on top — predicting future latent states conditioned on actions, without needing to retrain the encoder. ## Early Experiment ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/20aa04cd-1338-4032-bfd6-2a9aefce7c58/Screenshot_2026-03-02_at_10.00.46_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466V5C6XCYA%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T152300Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjED8aCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIBhaRZiLC7JWqcE%2Bb8TNWmYu08lIA4%2Bf4j6y7tOiXkfqAiEA522UGoQLzRTlyn2kP0JA3IM9oXJbKngJtRYqABid1eIq%2FwMICBAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDJi7gm6HOJ7GUvjhZSrcA41XbNYCIk1Cp9EDShJhFfrck1oKW5eAyoFAuWxJQ20tbcgCo%2BbvNPwdQywVkFN5%2BYdc4T%2Fqff4aP5m6VoAmCFphcBuQ5nT2NmlATGOlVU85JRkPVnUgMxnqtcruw3iUhidznzUx7lrjkVPQ%2BdiGONWmXDW%2BarhI1%2BZgHYhMruslxYrvXHaddwe%2B7trdOxYWRodldqSEQ%2Fq%2FS5Eq2CA2C8SGBjiyhEsg0gFWk8z3XJOxj%2FHzpIIJIBHRg%2FEu6niSSz%2Bsk8HFpeRlbNzkWgtvpz20gEcb%2BTNABPggxQHUIx78voW0UuXKZCtpbNffU4qJ8RXG%2BCvahLELrZKPDqsEh2frzowvWwC9PporknWksrwDnkn%2BLHBW7PiizL0N0sQhDd5KDXhXud5dnCwElQK1lsgy1wbLNUFe8bpCq%2FVKZb33W61tXfqkR3ZUqU4JjCO5s%2B6nTQatIfizLe4%2B1j6WgvIXiLoPusBltWhhUUiD2hMY1BfsH2WAydUftj2g%2Fp3y%2FwFEFVlz9UkVZVk8rhRoK9RiQJJv28%2BlHVzTQJXmY4GFk2hAtSbrsTgwmXv7aWktVq19b93FKJ91yqKnp%2FA202tJGma6mZlZ%2BfqnEypTmWYMEE8gRMW28dTniUY2MMDQk88GOqUBXOrN03AeSpKU0t3GdCZtxkP%2B8Fa6SHrENIKEDDZIJbLxnP2E2u2X3ubWUkzE8gBqCQhMEgQ90F1yM9BMLQU%2BcRfNoOZxEjzvxKwN3b5RP7fube52BhCNlJWiubsFSIU4qOQLPB%2FXVgsk5qbKpket916JGuIdPq0EqyEw%2F8IoB4V0cGgkP5NnhTjT4KcrmYylCIm6wZymKB49pYE9d86PLPJhRivk&X-Amz-Signature=bbdab2e24284b4c2d9c10944fc5825320073fa4fc41505b140e61e374569426c&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) *Fig 2: Our preliminary results. Attentive probe on SSv2 motion classification. DINO-style SSL gives \~7% improvement over baseline, and SSL accuracy is still going up at 150k steps while no-SSL has plateaued.* **Original Video** **No SSL** **SSL (DINO)** *PCA visualization of first 3 latents channels. The SSL latents look smoother and detailed than no SSL.* This already shows the encoder is picking up temporal-semantic structure from SSL. ## How we measure success - **rFID / rPSNR**: reconstruction shouldn't degrade much (≤10% vs rec-only baseline) - **Linear/attentive probe accuracy** (SSv2, Kinetics): semantic quality of latent space, should see clear gains - **gFID at fixed DiT budget**: does better latent → better generation? This is the key metric - **Convergence speed**: expect ≥2× faster downstream convergence vs rec-only VAE - **Scaling curve** (gFID vs VAE pre-training FLOPs): should be monotonically improving, not stagnating ## Expected artifacts - Pre-trained video tokenizer checkpoints at multiple scales - Training code + eval pipeline - Video SSL / V-JEPA training and evaluation setup (probe training, SSv2/Kinetics benchmarks) — reusable for future video SSL work and planning model development - Ablation data (SSL variants, loss weights, latent dims, scaling curves) ## Plan **Phase 1 — Exploration** - V-JEPA baseline with ViT is already running — SSv2 attentive probe accuracy (single temporal segment, 1 spatial view) at 300k steps: 43.9%. Still climbing.
Steps 50k 100k 150k 200k 250k 300k
**Accuracy** 39.9% 42.8% 42.0% 42.5% 43.8% 43.9%
- Next: match this with our Swin encoder — Swin's windowed attention is much more efficient to scale to high-res, long videos compared to ViT's quadratic global attention. Our Swin-base (slightly larger than ViT-base) with 2x temporal downsampling and 16x spatial (same as V-JEPA, which does it at patching) is already close early on:
Steps 20k 50k
**Swin (2x temporal, 16x spatial)** 35.2% 41.3%
- Then combine Swin V-JEPA with the VAE reconstruction objective — this is the core experiment - Sweep loss weights (λ_rec, λ_ssl) and batch sampling - Compare against E2E (REPA-E style end-to-end VAE+diffusion training) baseline - Establish scaling curves for each variant - Decision point: does the joint objective beat reconstruction-only at both probe accuracy and downstream generation? **Phase 2 — Scale-up** - Train final tokenizer at scale (Swin-L/XL encoder, large video dataset) - Full downstream diffusion eval - Test encoder reuse for conditioning ## Key References - [VTP: Towards Scalable Pre-training of Visual Tokenizers for Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13687) — Yao et al., 2025 - [REPA-E: Unlocking VAE for End-to-End Tuning with Latent Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10483) — Leng et al., 2025 - [RAE: Diffusion Transformers with Representation Autoencoders](https://rae-dit.github.io/) — Zheng et al., 2025 - [FLUX.2 VAE: Representation Comparison](https://bfl.ai/research/representation-comparison) — BFL blog, Nov 2025 - [Generative modelling in latent space](https://sander.ai/2025/04/15/latents.html) — Sander Dieleman, Apr 2025 - [V-JEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471) — Bardes et al., 2024 - [V-JEPA 2: Understanding, Prediction and Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) — Assran et al., 2025 Status Update — April 17, 2026 "}

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"🌇 Values Interview Guide","url":"https://www.notion.so/344c370222d581bba979ed7cafa1348c","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/344c370222d581bba979ed7cafa1348c as of 2026-04-16T10:52:24.026Z: {"title":"Values Interview Guide"} This guide helps interviewers assess candidates against our four core values. Each section covers one value, with a scoring matrix per question showing what strong, mixed, and weak answers look like. > **How to use this guide:** For each answer, assess both the value-specific signals and the universal signals at the bottom of this page. A strong answer is specific, concise, and shows genuine ownership. --- #### Contents (quick find) {toggle="true"} # 🔥 Obsessed We are a frontier research lab. The science has to be right, the understanding deep, the product beautiful. #### Q1 — Walk me through how you've improved at your craft over the past year. What specifically did you do?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Names a specific skill gap they identified themselves, unprompted Genuine effort but driven by a manager's feedback, not own initiative Struggles to name anything concrete from the past year, references articles, books but nothing concrete even when pressed
Describes a deliberate practice: course, mentor, side project, applied reading Learning happened but no clear application or output to point to Describes general busyness as the reason for not improving
Can show output — shipped thing, measurable result, changed habit Improvement was broad ("I tried to communicate better") without specifics Vague platitudes: "I always try to keep learning"
Improvement was self-directed, not performance-review driven Only cites on-the-job experience, no intentional self-investment
### Q2 — Describe a time you went back and redid something even though it was "good enough."
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
The redo was self-initiated — nobody asked, no deadline pressure Redo was triggered by user feedback or a bug, not proactively self driven Can't recall a specific example — defaults to "I usually just ship it"
Can articulate precisely what they identified as the additional opportunity and why they invested the time- what they identified as the value add Knew something was off but waited until it caused a problem Frames "good enough" as the right standard without tension
The outcome was meaningfully better, and they can describe how Redid it but can't explain what specifically made it better Example is trivial or clearly hypothetical, not a real trade-off
Shows pride in the work, not just in the efficiency of delivering it
### Q3 — Tell me about a time you pushed back on shipping because you thought something wasn't ready.
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Articulates clearly what the risk was and why they personally felt it was wrong Did raise the concern but backed down quickly when pushed No example — always deferred to the team or PM on readiness
Pushed back despite pressures from: peers, manager, or deadlines Concern was process or coverage, not about the quality of the product Describes pushback as conflict-avoidant: "I mentioned it but didn't want to block"
Used data or a concrete argument, not just a gut feeling Framing is more about covering all bases (self serving in nature) than genuine care for the outcome Example is about missing a test, not genuine quality conviction
Outcome validates the concern, or they accept the cost if overruled
--- # 🤝 Low Ego The work speaks. The best idea wins, no matter who said it. Credit is shared. Nobody is above any task. ### Q1 — Describe a situation where you were wrong about something important. How did you realise it and change course?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
The mistake was significant — technical direction, architecture, people decision Admits the mistake but still somewhat frames it as "not entirely my fault" Example feels transparently chosen to look good — the "mistake" had a great outcome
They realised it themselves or genuinely accepted it when shown evidence/ provided with rational Changed course but waited until it was unavoidable to do so Extensive reframing, context-setting, or blame-sharing before getting to the error
Changed course visibly and without hedging or minimising Example is low-stakes — admits being wrong about something minor Can't recall a genuinely wrong call, or pivots to someone else's mistake
Reflects on what they'd do differently- no defensiveness
### Q2 — Tell me about a time you received critical feedback that was hard to hear.
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Feedback was substantive — about work quality, behaviour, or judgment, not just style Accepted the feedback but the change was surface-level or short-lived Describes immediately agreeing with feedback — no evidence of genuine reflection or investment in personal growth/ development as a result
First reaction may have been defensive, and they acknowledge that honestly Describes listening but doesn't show evidence it actually changed anything Spends most of the answer explaining why the feedback was partly wrong
Sat with it, came back to it, changed something specific as a result Feedback was from a peer they already disagreed with — complicated by the relationship Chose an example where the feedback was ultimately unfair or incorrect
Grateful for the feedback in hindsight, even if it stung
### Q3 — Tell me about a project or decision you'd handle differently in hindsight.
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Specific, real trade-off — not a humble-brag disguised as a mistake Genuine reflection but framed mostly as bad luck or context, not judgment Humble-brag: "I worked too hard" or "I cared too much"
Clear-eyed about what they got wrong and why they got it wrong at the time "Different" would be only tactical — same strategic call, different execution The "mistake" was driven entirely by someone else
Can name what they'd do differently without over-qualifying Learning is vague: "I'd communicate more" without specifics No real answer — "I think I made the right call given what I knew"
Shows updated mental model, not just regret
--- # ⚡ Bold We take the ambitious bet. We ship, we do not wait for conditions to be perfect. ### Q1 — Tell me about a time you made a decision with incomplete information. What was at stake?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Stakes were real — could have cost them time, credibility, money, or a relationship Made the call but spent most energy gathering more information first Escalated to a manager or committee rather than deciding themselves
They name the specific unknowns and explain what they did to reduce the risk Moved forward but the stakes were low — it was safe to be bold Waited until they had enough information that it no longer felt uncertain
Moved despite the gap, didn't wait to have full certainty Outcome was bad and they're still justifying the decision rather than learning from it Example is low-stakes or hypothetical, not a real personal decision
Reflects on the decision quality separately from the outcome
### Q2 — Have you ever proposed or championed a significant change that was initially unpopular?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Named the resistance clearly — who pushed back, why, and what the stakes were Proposed it but dropped it quickly when it met resistance Can't recall championing anything that faced real resistance
Continued to champion it even when unpopular, not just floated the idea once Change happened but driven by someone more senior — they just supported it Only advocates for ideas once consensus is forming — not before
Had a view on why they were right even when others disagreed Unpopularity was minor or the change was low-risk Describes it as "raising concerns" rather than driving change
Won people over through evidence and persistence, not politics
### Q3 — When have you stepped into a role or responsibility you weren't fully qualified for?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Didn't wait to be handed the opportunity — actively took it or created it Stepped in but only because they were asked, not self-initiated Waited to be fully qualified before taking on new scope
Gap was real, not just imposter syndrome — they were genuinely underprepared Gap was modest — mostly a title change, not a real stretch Example is a stretch in name only — they were clearly ready for it
Describes how they filled the gap: who they leaned on, what they learned fast Made it work but by playing it safe rather than leaning into the challenge Describes the role as handed to them with full support and no real risk
--- # 💛 Kind People over politics. We treat each other with genuine warmth. Agency without empathy creates chaos. ### Q1 — How do you ensure new team members feel welcome and foster an inclusive environment?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Names specific things they personally do — not policies or team programs Describes what the team does rather than what they personally do Delegates this to HR, onboarding docs, or the manager
Gives examples of noticing when someone was struggling and reaching out Effort is reactive — responds when asked, doesn't proactively notice Describes a good culture without any personal contribution to it
Thinks about psychological safety as a precondition for good work, not just niceness Actions are performative: coffee chats, Slack welcomes — no depth to the relationship Answer is abstract and values-performative: "I believe in inclusion"
Inclusive behaviour shows up even when it costs them time or attention
### Q2 — What does a positive team culture look like to you, and how do you personally contribute to it?
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Definition of good culture is specific and earned; refers to lived experiences Good definition of culture but contribution is passive — "I try not to create drama" Describes culture they've wanted to work in, not culture they've helped build
Contribution is behavioural and consistent, not just in good moments Contribution sounds like hygiene, not leadership — follows norms rather than sets them No personal ownership — culture is something that happens to them
Shows how they behave when culture is under stress — conflict, deadlines, failure Culture described in terms of perks or vibes rather than trust and accountability Clichés only: "open door policy," "psychological safety" without real substance
Connects team health directly to the quality of work produced
### Q3 — Tell me about a time you went out of your way to help a colleague succeed — not because it was your job.
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Help came at a real cost to them — time, visibility, competing priorities Helped because asked, not because they noticed Example is really a team collaboration, not personal sacrifice
Noticed the need themselves rather than being asked Cost was low — helped in a way that also benefited them Describes mentoring or code review as extraordinary — these are normal
The colleague's success mattered to them intrinsically, not strategically The relationship was close — natural to help, not a stretch Framing centres their own effort: "I really went above and beyond" rather than the colleague's outcome
Stays humble about the impact — not self-congratulatory in the telling
--- # 📋 Universal Signals *Apply these to every answer, regardless of which value is being assessed.*
✅ Strong 🟡 Mixed ❌ Weak
Specific situation, named clearly Real example but takes too long to land Hypothetical or generic ("I usually…")
Concise — arrives at the point fast Credit or blame shared with others heavily Long preamble, vague example, no resolution
Owns their part without hedging Insight present but stated, not demonstrated Answer chosen to look good, not be honest
Outcome described, learning extracted Outcome unclear or not connected to the action No personal ownership anywhere in the answer
Natural delivery, not rehearsed Asks "what kind of answer are you looking for?"
"}

title: Vision for Training Cluster Team: Making 10,000+ GPU Training Reliable, Fast, and Effortless
content:
{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Vision for Training Cluster Team: Making 10,000+ GPU Training Reliable, Fast, and Effortless","url":"https://www.notion.so/33dc370222d58066b082cd55981dae1a","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/33dc370222d58066b082cd55981dae1a as of 2026-04-09T07:01:11.084Z: {"title":"Vision for Training Cluster Team: *Making 10,000+ GPU Training Reliable, Fast, and Effortless*"} # **Summary** We are entering a critical inflection point. The race to frontier-scale AI training is being won or lost on infrastructure. Our ability to train the next generation of models depends not just on acquiring GPUs, but on our ability to operate them at scale with maximum utilization, minimum downtime, and zero tolerance for wasted compute. This memo outlines our team’s charter: to build the systems foundation that makes frontier training runs routine, not heroic. We are organized around two reinforcing pillars - Resiliency and Scalability - with the goal of turning our GPU fleet into a reliable, high-throughput training factory. **The Core Problem** > At 10,000+ GPU scale, component failure is not an edge case - it is a statistical certainty on every training run. A single wasted wall-clock hour on a 10,000-GPU job is not one hour lost - it is 10,000 GPU-hours burned, the equivalent of running a single GPU continuously for over thirteen months. A single undetected straggler node can silently degrade throughput by 10–30%. An unrecoverable failure on a multi-day run can waste tens of thousands of GPU-hours. Our mission is to make these problems invisible to researchers. {color="red_bg"} --- # **Two Axes of Scale** We are scaling simultaneously along two axes, and each multiplies the complexity of the other: - **Total GPUs in fleet: **Growing cluster size from thousands to tens of thousands of GPUs. This increases the blast radius of systemic issues (firmware bugs, network misconfigurations, storage bottlenecks) and demands fleet-grade operational tooling. - **GPUs per training job: **Scaling individual jobs to consume thousands of GPUs simultaneously. This tightens coupling between nodes, makes collective communication a first-class scaling bottleneck, and means a single faulty node can stall the entire job. The intersection of these axes is where frontier training lives - and where most infrastructure teams break. Our charter is to ensure we don’t.
**Dimension** **Current State** **Near-Term Target** **Why It Matters**
Cluster Scale Scaling up 5K–20K GPUs per cluster Enables frontier-class training runs
Per-Job Scale Scaling up Full-cluster utilization Unlocks models that require massive parallelism
Mean Time to Recovery Reactive Automated sub-minute recovery Prevents 1000s of GPU-hours wasted per incident
GPU Utilization (MFU) Baseline \>55% sustained MFU Direct cost multiplier on \$100M+ infrastructure
# **Pillar 1: Resiliency** At scale, reliability is not about preventing every failure - it is about detecting failures instantly, recovering automatically, and ensuring no researcher has to debug infrastructure. Our resiliency strategy spans four layers: ## **1.1 Proactive Health Agent** We are building and owning a purpose-built health agent for our GPU fleet, developed in close partnership with NVIDIA to ensure CSP-agnostic operation. This is a strategic investment: rather than depending on any single cloud provider’s monitoring, we control our own detection and remediation stack. **Key Capabilities** - **Preflight checks: **Automated GPU/NIC/NVLink/storage validation before any node enters the schedulable pool. No job should ever land on a degraded node. - **Continuous background checks: **Persistent health probes running alongside workloads - detecting degradation (ECC errors, thermal throttling, NVLink CRC errors) before it becomes a failure. - **Active check harness: **On-demand deep diagnostics triggered on suspicious nodes: DCGM validation, NCCL loopback tests, memory stress, storage I/O benchmarks. - **CSP-agnostic design: **Portable across infrastructure providers. We are not locked into any vendor’s health monitoring stack. ## **1.2 Comprehensive Logging Infrastructure** Effective root-cause analysis at scale requires complete, correlated logs. We capture and centralize: - **GPU error history: **XID error codes per node with temporal correlation - enabling us to identify nodes trending toward failure before they crash a job. - **Node lifecycle events: **Every allocation, deallocation, reboot, and drain event - providing a full audit trail for any node involved in an incident. - **System-level logs: **syslog, kern.log, dmesg, and access.log captured and stored for every node. These are the forensic record when something goes wrong. ## **1.3 Unified Monitoring & Observability** Monitoring at this scale requires more than dashboards. It requires a single pane of glass that spans the entire fleet and provides both operator and researcher visibility: **Operator View: Global Fleet Dashboard** - Unified cross-cluster view of fleet health, node status, and active incidents - Anomaly detection and alerting across all clusters from a single control plane **Researcher View: Resource Dashboard** - Per-user and per-job visibility into all allocated resources - Storage consumption, CPU/memory utilization, and GPU metrics (memory, power draw, temperature, SM utilization) - Goal: researchers should never need to SSH into a node to understand their job’s behavior **Distributed Tracing & Correlation** - End-to-end request tracing from application layer through NCCL collectives down to individual NICs and switches - When a 4,000-GPU job degrades, we need to pinpoint the offending component in minutes, not hours # **Pillar 2: Scalability (The Scaling Factory)** Scaling a training run from 256 to 8,192 GPUs is not a linear exercise. Every component in the stack has a breaking point, and finding those breaking points after a job launches is unacceptable. We are building a systematic testing and validation framework - a Scaling Factory - that stress-tests every component independently before it is relied upon in production. ## **2.1 Component-Level Scale Testing Harness** A modular harness for isolating and benchmarking individual subsystems at target scale: - **Memory checkpointing: **Benchmark checkpoint write and restore throughput at target scale. At 10K GPUs, a synchronized checkpoint can generate terabytes of I/O in seconds - this must not become a bottleneck. - **Data loading pipelines: **Stress-test ingestion from both centralized data lakes and distributed local stores (e.g., AIStore). Validate that data loading never starves the training loop. - **Collective communication (NCCL): **Profile allreduce, allgather, and reduce-scatter at target GPU counts across the actual network topology. Identify bandwidth and latency cliffs before production. - **Compute-communication overlap: **Validate that the training framework effectively overlaps gradient computation with NCCL collectives. Poor overlap is the most common cause of low MFU at scale. ## **2.2 Network Fabric & Topology** At frontier scale, the network is the computer. We must own the performance and reliability of the interconnect: - Topology-aware job placement to keep all-to-all traffic within the same spine/rail where possible - Congestion monitoring and adaptive routing across InfiniBand/RoCE fabrics - Network partition detection and automated traffic rerouting - Per-job network performance baselines to detect degradation early ## **2.3 Job-Level Resiliency** A frontier training run is a multi-day, multi-thousand-GPU commitment. It must be resilient to the failures that will inevitably occur during that window: - **Straggler identification: **Real-time detection of nodes performing below the cohort - whether due to thermal throttling, degraded NVLinks, or noisy-neighbor effects. Automated eviction and replacement without job restart. - **Node failure recovery: **Hot-spare pools and automated node substitution so that a single GPU failure does not kill a multi-day run. Seamless checkpoint restore onto replacement nodes. - **Elastic training support: **Where frameworks support it, the ability to continue training with a reduced node count while a replacement is provisioned, rather than blocking the entire job. # **Pillar 3: Scheduling & Resource Orchestration** As both cluster size and per-job GPU count grow, intelligent scheduling becomes a force multiplier for utilization and throughput: - **Topology-aware placement: **Ensure large jobs are placed on physically adjacent nodes to minimize network hops and maximize bisection bandwidth. - **Gang scheduling: **Guarantee that all GPUs for a job are allocated atomically - partial allocations waste resources and block other jobs. - **Multi-tenancy & fairness: **Enforce fair-share policies so that no single team monopolizes the cluster while others queue. Priority tiers for frontier training runs vs. experimentation. - **Preemption & backfill: **Intelligent preemption of lower-priority jobs with checkpoint-and-resume, combined with backfill scheduling to keep GPUs warm during gaps. # **Pillar 4: Fleet Lifecycle & Capacity Management** A fleet of 10,000+ GPUs is not static. It requires deliberate lifecycle management: - **Node qualification & burn-in: **Every new node passes a standardized qualification pipeline (stress tests, NCCL benchmarks, storage I/O) before entering the schedulable pool. - **Firmware & driver rollouts: **Staged rollout strategy for NVIDIA driver and firmware updates - canary, soak, and fleet-wide phases with automated rollback on regression. - **Capacity planning: **Forward-looking models for GPU demand based on training roadmap, so procurement and provisioning stay ahead of research needs. - **Decommissioning: **Graceful retirement of nodes that exceed failure rate thresholds, with data wipe and audit trail. # **Execution Roadmap** ## **Near-Term (0–3 months): Foundation** - Deploy health agent v1 with preflight and continuous background checks across all clusters - Centralize logging pipeline (XID, lifecycle, syslog, kern.log, dmesg) with 90-day retention - Launch unified global fleet dashboard and per-researcher resource dashboard - Stand up Scaling Factory harness with checkpoint, data loading, and NCCL benchmarks - Implement straggler detection with automated alerting (manual eviction) - Establish node qualification pipeline for new hardware ## **Medium-Term (3–6 months): Automation** - Automated straggler eviction and node replacement without job restart - End-to-end distributed tracing from application layer to network fabric - Topology-aware scheduling with gang scheduling and fair-share enforcement - Staged firmware rollout pipeline with automated regression detection - Checkpoint I/O optimization to handle synchronized 10K+ GPU checkpoint storms ## **Long-Term (6–12 months): Autonomy** - Fully self-healing fleet: predictive failure detection, preemptive node drain, and automated hot-spare substitution - Elastic training support: seamless scale-down and scale-up during running jobs - ML-driven capacity planning tied to the research training roadmap - Sub-5-minute mean-time-to-recovery for any single-node failure in a frontier training run # **Why This Matters Now** Every hour of GPU downtime at our scale represents a direct cost in both dollars and competitive position. The teams that win at frontier AI training will not be the ones with the most GPUs - they will be the ones that extract the most value from every GPU-hour. Our infrastructure must be a competitive advantage, not a bottleneck. This team exists to make frontier-scale training runs routine. We are building the systems, the tooling, and the operational muscle to ensure that when a researcher launches a 10,000-GPU job, they can trust that the infrastructure will hold. ### **Our Mandate** Researchers should think about models, not machines. Every hour spent debugging infrastructure is an hour not spent pushing the frontier. We own that problem, completely. {color="green_bg"} --- "}

Recommended Standard for most Usecases = Flux.2 \[pro\] 2. Best Model = Flux.2 \[max\] 3. Fastest = Flux.2 \[schnell\] (Upcoming Model) 4. Cheapest = look it up for [API pricing](https://bfl.ai/pricing) & [licensing pricing](https://bfl.ai/licensing) 5. High resolution = Flux.2 \[pro\] Ultra (up to 4 megapixel, all other images 1 mp) 6. Edits = Flux.2 \[flex\] 7. Saturated style (liked by consumers) = Flux.2 \[pro\] 8. Self-host = Flux.2 \[dev\] or Flux.2 \[klein\] (upcoming) 9. How does moderation work? [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-Fn8bdZzxT5nWCfprIx_eLM7QahgZmysrKC9EknGfRU/edit?tab=t.0](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-Fn8bdZzxT5nWCfprIx_eLM7QahgZmysrKC9EknGfRU/edit?tab=t.0) **→ Flux.2 \[pro\] is our Flagship workhorse model, in most cases you cannot do much wrong recommending that one!** Model Strengths and Limitations, New data source, and New data source ## Deployment Recommendations Sometimes we provide inference containers or code that customers deploy directly on their infrastructure. If they ask about number of GPUs to use for their deployment, this is usually what we recommend:
Model # of GPUs Type of GPU Additional Considerations
FLUX.2 \[pro\] 4 H100, H200 or GB200 Fewer GPUs could lead to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors for larger images or higher numbers of reference images, as well as higher latency. Smaller GPUs (in terms of memory) could suffer from the same issue.
FLUX.2 \[flex\] 4 H200 or GB200 H100 GPUs don’t suffice for the current setup in terms of memory. Fewer and smaller GPUs might suffer from increased latency and OOM errors.
FLUX.2 \[klein\] 4B & 9B 1 H100, H200 or GB200 Klein can run on a single GPU. Using more than a single GPU will not reduce latency further, and smaller GPUs could suffer from OOM errors.
## FLUX Model Names and what they mean - Number = version & sub version (.1, 1.1, .2) - \[pro\] vs \[dev\] = closed source (API) vs. open weights (licensing & self-host) - Ultra = High resolution (currently up to 4 megapixel) - Raw = Fine-tuned for ultra realistic output ## FLUX .2 FLUX.2 \[max\] - Top-Tier-Quality Image Generation and Editing FLUX.2 Prompting Guide \[WIP\] ## [FLUX.1 Kontext](/1fcc370222d580e2af0df93271590e2b?pvs=25) FLUX.1 Kontext \[max\] - Doesn’t do much for edits - basically built on pro and has a model behind it and picks what it thinks are best. (secret) - Thats why it costs more - Helps a lot more with text to image - Likely better for text FLUX.1 Kontext \[pro\] - best overall for price and performance likley (don’t share this with customers!!!) FLUX.1 Kontext \[dev\] (open weights - [FLUX non-commercial license](https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux/blob/main/model_licenses/LICENSE-FLUX1-dev)) ## FLUX1.1 FLUX1.1 \[pro\] - more stylized and less resolution FLUX1.1 \[pro\] Ultra - Based off 1.1. It can go much higher resolution than every model. - Ultra can do 4mp (2k res) image so resolution is way higher. - Still very fast speed. - Worse at listening and prompt following than Kontext (personal preference) FLUX1.1 \[pro\] Raw & ## FLUX.1 Flux .1 pro is sunsetted.
